problems.title: Zero central torque fixes an orbital plane
problems.objective: Use the torque equation to prove angular-momentum conservation and identify the geometric edge case of purely radial motion.
problems.statement: A particle of mass $m$ moves under a central force $\mathbf F(\mathbf r)=f(r)\hat{\mathbf r}$, with $r>0$. Starting from $d\mathbf L/dt=\mathbf r\times\mathbf F$, prove that the motion lies in a fixed plane when $\mathbf L\ne0$. State carefully what remains true when $\mathbf L=0$.
problems.strategy: First identify the torque direction, then use the constant normal vector supplied by nonzero angular momentum, and finally separate the radial zero-angular-momentum case.
permittedResults: Angular momentum about the force center is $\mathbf L=\mathbf r\times m\dot{\mathbf r}$.
hints: Evaluate $\mathbf r\times f(r)\hat{\mathbf r}$ before discussing the trajectory.
For nonzero $\mathbf L$, compute $\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf L$.
If $\mathbf L=0$, ask whether one unique plane is selected or whether the motion is radial.
rubricCriteria: Shows that the central torque vanishes and hence that $\mathbf L$ is a constant vector.
Uses $\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf L=0$ to identify the fixed plane perpendicular to nonzero $\mathbf L$.
Treats $\mathbf L=0$ separately as radial motion and does not claim that a unique orbital plane is determined.

commonErrors.description: Claims that a radial force is parallel to the velocity.
commonErrors.consequence: Central means parallel to position, so the torque conclusion is lost by an unjustified velocity assumption.

commonErrors.description: Uses a plane normal to $\mathbf L$ even when $\mathbf L=0$.
commonErrors.consequence: The zero vector supplies no unique normal; the radial trajectory can be embedded in infinitely many planes.

problems.solution: Because $\mathbf r=r\hat{\mathbf r}$, $d\mathbf L/dt=\mathbf r\times f(r)\hat{\mathbf r}=\mathbf0$. Thus $\mathbf L$ is constant. Also $\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf L=\mathbf r\cdot(\mathbf r\times m\dot{\mathbf r})=0$, so if $\mathbf L\ne0$, every position lies in the fixed plane through the force center perpendicular to $\mathbf L$. If $\mathbf L=0$, then $\mathbf r\times\dot{\mathbf r}=0$: away from $r=0$ the velocity is radial and the path lies on a fixed radial line, but no unique plane is selected.
problems.flawedProof: A central force is always tangent to the orbit, so $\mathbf r\times\mathbf F=0$. Therefore every orbit, including one with $\mathbf L=0$, has a unique plane perpendicular to $\mathbf L$.

problems.title: The centripetal sign is radial, not optional
problems.objective: Compute the signed radial acceleration and central force for uniform circular motion with a declared outward convention.
problems.statement: A $4.00\,\mathrm{kg}$ particle moves counterclockwise at constant speed $3.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$ on a circle of radius $2.00\,\mathrm m$ centered at the force origin. Take $\hat{\mathbf r}$ outward. Find $a_r$, the central force vector, and the torque about the origin. Check the units and explain why the direction of motion does not change the force direction.
problems.strategy: Use the outward-positive radial component, multiply by the mass, and then evaluate the moment arm cross the radial force.
permittedResults: For uniform circular motion, $\mathbf a=-(v^2/r)\hat{\mathbf r}$.
hints: With outward positive, the radial component is $a_r=-v^2/r$.
Use $\mathbf F=m\mathbf a$ without discarding the unit vector.
A radial force has zero cross product with its position vector.
rubricCriteria: Computes $a_r$ with the correct inward sign and SI acceleration units.
Gives the force as a signed vector with magnitude and newton units.
Finds zero torque and explains that clockwise versus counterclockwise motion leaves the inward acceleration unchanged.

commonErrors.description: Reports $a_r=+v^2/r$ with outward positive.
commonErrors.consequence: The acceleration would point away from the circle center and could not maintain the orbit.

commonErrors.description: Assigns the force a tangential direction because the particle moves counterclockwise.
commonErrors.consequence: Uniform speed requires no tangential acceleration; only the velocity direction changes.

problems.solution: $a_r=-(3.00\,\mathrm{m/s})^2/(2.00\,\mathrm m)=-4.50\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, so $\mathbf F=m\mathbf a=-18.0\,\mathrm N\,\hat{\mathbf r}$. The torque is $\boldsymbol\tau=\mathbf r\times\mathbf F=\mathbf0$. Reversing the tangential velocity reverses angular momentum but not the inward centripetal acceleration.
problems.flawedProof: $a_r=v^2/r=4.50\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ outward. Counterclockwise motion therefore needs a counterclockwise tangential force of $18.0\,\mathrm N$.

problems.title: Radial speed contributes no angular momentum
problems.objective: Separate radial and transverse velocity to compute angular momentum and areal velocity.
problems.statement: In plane polar coordinates, a $0.800\,\mathrm{kg}$ particle is at $r=2.50\,\mathrm m$ with $\dot r=-1.20\,\mathrm{m/s}$ and $r\dot\phi=4.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Find the signed angular momentum for increasing $\phi$, the areal velocity, and the value each would have if only $\dot r$ changed sign.
problems.strategy: Resolve velocity into radial and azimuthal parts, retain only the transverse part in the cross product, and relate swept area to $r^2\dot\phi/2$.
hints: The cross product of $\mathbf r$ with $\dot r\hat{\mathbf r}$ is zero.
Use the given transverse speed directly in $L_z=mr v_\phi$.
Changing only $\dot r$ does not change $\dot\phi$.
rubricCriteria: Computes $L_z=8.00\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}$ with the sign set by increasing $\phi$.
Computes $dA/dt=5.00\,\mathrm{m^2/s}$ with correct units.
Explains that reversing only the radial component changes neither result.

commonErrors.description: Uses the total speed $\sqrt{\dot r^2+v_\phi^2}$ in $mr v$.
commonErrors.consequence: The radial component is incorrectly counted even though it is parallel to the position vector.

commonErrors.description: Sets the angular momentum negative because $\dot r<0$.
commonErrors.consequence: The angular-momentum sign is controlled by azimuthal motion, not inward versus outward radial motion.

problems.solution: $L_z=mr v_\phi=(0.800)(2.50)(4.00)=8.00\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}$. The areal velocity is $L_z/(2m)=8.00/(1.600)=5.00\,\mathrm{m^2/s}$. Reversing $\dot r$ leaves both values unchanged because radial velocity has zero moment arm cross product.
problems.flawedProof: The speed is $\sqrt{1.20^2+4.00^2}=4.18\,\mathrm{m/s}$, so $L=mr v=8.35\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}$. Reversing $\dot r$ reverses $L$.

problems.title: Equal areas require unequal angular speeds
problems.objective: Use conserved specific angular momentum to compare angular speeds at different radii.
problems.statement: A central-force orbit has constant specific angular momentum $h=r^2\dot\phi=12.0\,\mathrm{m^2/s}$. Compare $\dot\phi$ at $r_1=3.00\,\mathrm m$ and $r_2=6.00\,\mathrm m$. Find the area swept in $0.500\,\mathrm s$ at either location and explain the result without assuming a circular orbit.
problems.strategy: Solve $r^2\dot\phi=h$ at each radius, then use $dA/dt=h/2$ rather than arc length.
hints: Angular speed scales as $r^{-2}$ when $h$ is fixed.
The swept area rate is one half of $h$.
No constant-radius assumption is needed for the instantaneous area formula.
rubricCriteria: Finds $\dot\phi_1=1.33\,\mathrm{rad/s}$ and $\dot\phi_2=0.333\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.
Finds a swept area of $3.00\,\mathrm{m^2}$ in either half-second interval.
Connects the factor-four angular-speed change to constant areal velocity, not to circular motion.

commonErrors.description: Assumes $r\dot\phi$ rather than $r^2\dot\phi$ is conserved.
commonErrors.consequence: This confuses transverse speed with angular momentum and gives only a factor-two change.

commonErrors.description: Uses sector area $\pi r^2$ for the half-second sweep.
commonErrors.consequence: A full-circle area is unrelated to the local swept-area rate on a general orbit.

problems.solution: $\dot\phi_1=h/r_1^2=12.0/9.00=1.33\,\mathrm{rad/s}$ and $\dot\phi_2=12.0/36.0=0.333\,\mathrm{rad/s}$, so the nearer angular speed is four times larger. Since $dA/dt=h/2=6.00\,\mathrm{m^2/s}$, either interval sweeps $3.00\,\mathrm{m^2}$. These are instantaneous relations valid even while $r$ changes.
problems.flawedProof: The tangential speed is conserved, so doubling the radius halves the angular speed. The swept area is therefore larger at $r=6.00\,\mathrm m$.

problems.title: Differentiate the effective potential with its sign intact
problems.objective: Derive the one-dimensional radial equation from energy and identify the centrifugal contribution with correct dimensions.
problems.statement: For a particle of mass $m$ in a time-independent central potential $U(r)$ with nonzero angular momentum magnitude $\ell$, define $U_{\mathrm{eff}}(r)=U(r)+\ell^2/(2mr^2)$. Differentiate the radial energy equation to obtain the radial equation of motion. State the dimensions of each term and the physical sign of the angular-momentum contribution.
problems.strategy: Write the conserved energy as radial kinetic plus effective potential, differentiate along a nonturning segment, and then extend the result by continuity through turning points.
hints: After factoring $\dot r$, the force is $-dU_{\mathrm{eff}}/dr$.
rubricCriteria: Differentiates the conserved radial energy without changing the sign of the $r^{-2}$ term.
Obtains $m\ddot r=-U'(r)+\ell^2/(mr^3)$ and explains continuity at a turning point.
Identifies the angular-momentum term as an outward force and audits energy and force dimensions.

commonErrors.description: Writes the effective potential with a negative centrifugal term.
commonErrors.consequence: The angular-momentum barrier becomes spuriously attractive and predicts collapse for large $\ell$.

commonErrors.description: Divides by $\dot r$ and declares the equation invalid at every turning point.
commonErrors.consequence: The equation holds by continuity even where the instantaneous radial speed vanishes.

problems.solution: $0=dE/dt=\dot r[m\ddot r+U'(r)-\ell^2/(mr^3)]$. Hence on intervals with $\dot r\ne0$, $m\ddot r=-U'(r)+\ell^2/(mr^3)$, and smoothness extends this identity through ordinary turning points. Both $U$ and $\ell^2/(2mr^2)$ have joule units; their radial derivatives have newton units. The positive $\ell^2/(mr^3)$ term points outward and creates the centrifugal barrier.
problems.flawedProof: Because $d(r^{-2})/dr=+2r^{-3}$, the effective force is $-U'(r)-\ell^2/(mr^3)$, so angular momentum adds an inward force.

problems.title: A logarithmic potential has a flat rotation curve
problems.objective: Derive the radius-independent circular speed of a logarithmic central potential and compute an orbital period with unit conversion.
problems.statement: A particle of mass $m$ moves in $U(r)=m v_0^2\ln(r/r_0)$, where $v_0=180\,\mathrm{km/s}$. Derive the central force and the circular speed at radius $r$. Then find the period of a circular orbit at $r=8.00\,\mathrm{kpc}$, using $1\,\mathrm{kpc}=3.086\times10^{19}\,\mathrm m$ and $1\,\mathrm{Myr}=3.156\times10^{13}\,\mathrm s$.
problems.strategy: Differentiate the potential, equate inward force magnitude to $mv_c^2/r$, and convert both radius and speed before evaluating $2\pi r/v_c$.
hints: $d\ln(r/r_0)/dr=1/r$; the reference radius drops out of the force.
Convert $180\,\mathrm{km/s}$ to $1.80\times10^5\,\mathrm{m/s}$ before finding the period.
rubricCriteria: Derives $\mathbf F=-(m v_0^2/r)\hat{\mathbf r}$ and $v_c=v_0$.
Converts the stated radius and evaluates the period numerically.
Reports $T\approx8.62\times10^{15}\,\mathrm s\approx273\,\mathrm{Myr}$ and notes the flat rotation curve.

commonErrors.description: Differentiates $\ln(r/r_0)$ as $r_0/r$.
commonErrors.consequence: The force acquires a dimensionful factor and the circular-speed result is corrupted.

commonErrors.description: Combines kiloparsecs with kilometres per second without conversion.
commonErrors.consequence: The reported period has no coherent time unit and is wrong by large powers of ten.

problems.solution: $dU/dr=m v_0^2/r$, so $\mathbf F=-(m v_0^2/r)\hat{\mathbf r}$. Circular balance gives $m v_c^2/r=m v_0^2/r$, hence $v_c=v_0$ at every radius. Here $r=2.4688\times10^{20}\,\mathrm m$ and $v_0=1.80\times10^5\,\mathrm{m/s}$, so $T=2\pi r/v_0=8.62\times10^{15}\,\mathrm s=273\,\mathrm{Myr}$.
problems.flawedProof: $F=-m v_0^2r_0/r$, so $v_c^2=v_0^2r_0$ and the circular speed depends on the arbitrary logarithm reference scale.

problems.title: Kepler turning radii come from one quadratic
problems.objective: Use instantaneous polar data to compute energy, angular momentum, and both radial turning points in an attractive inverse-square potential.
problems.statement: A $1.00\,\mathrm{kg}$ particle moves in $U(r)=-k/r$ with $k=20.0\,\mathrm{J\,m}$. At $r=4.00\,\mathrm m$, it has $\dot r=1.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$ and transverse speed $v_\phi=2.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Find $E$, $\ell$, and all positive turning radii. Classify the orbit as bound or unbound.
problems.strategy: Compute the full kinetic energy and angular momentum from the snapshot, then solve $E=U_{\mathrm{eff}}(r)$ with $\dot r=0$.
hints: Include both $\dot r^2$ and $v_\phi^2$ in the kinetic energy.
Multiply the turning-point equation by $r^2$ and retain both positive roots.
rubricCriteria: Computes $E=-2.50\,\mathrm J$ and $\ell=8.00\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}$.
Solves the correct quadratic to obtain $r_-=2.21\,\mathrm m$ and $r_+=5.79\,\mathrm m$.
Uses $E<0$ with two finite turning radii to classify the orbit as bound.

commonErrors.description: Omits radial kinetic energy from the snapshot energy.
commonErrors.consequence: The wrong energy produces incorrect turning radii.

commonErrors.description: Solves $E=U(r)$ and ignores the angular-momentum barrier.
commonErrors.consequence: The periapsis is lost and the inferred orbit can reach an inaccessible radius.

problems.solution: $E=\tfrac12(1.00)(1.00^2+2.00^2)-20.0/4.00=-2.50\,\mathrm J$ and $\ell=(1.00)(4.00)(2.00)=8.00\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}$. At a turning point, $-2.50=-20.0/r+32.0/r^2$, or $2.50r^2-20.0r+32.0=0$. Thus $r=(20.0\pm\sqrt{80.0})/5.00$, giving $2.21\,\mathrm m$ and $5.79\,\mathrm m$. Negative energy and two finite apsides imply a bound ellipse.
problems.flawedProof: $E=\tfrac12v_\phi^2-k/r=-3.00\,\mathrm J$. Turning points satisfy $E=-k/r$, so the only one is $r=6.67\,\mathrm m$.

problems.title: Escape from a softened gravitational center
problems.objective: Derive escape speed from a finite central potential and check the point-mass limit.
problems.statement: The potential per unit mass is $\Phi(r)=-\mu/\sqrt{r^2+a^2}$ with $\Phi(\infty)=0$. Derive the minimum local escape speed. Evaluate it for $\mu=4.00\times10^{14}\,\mathrm{m^3/s^2}$, $r=6.00\times10^6\,\mathrm m$, and $a=2.00\times10^6\,\mathrm m$. Check the limit $a\to0$.
problems.strategy: Set the specific energy of the marginal escaping trajectory to zero, solve for speed, and then inspect the zero-softening limit.
permittedResults: Escape with zero speed at infinity has specific energy $\varepsilon=0$.
rubricCriteria: Derives $v_{\mathrm{esc}}=\sqrt{2\mu/\sqrt{r^2+a^2}}$.
Evaluates $v_{\mathrm{esc}}\approx1.12\times10^4\,\mathrm{m/s}$ with correct units.
Recovers the point-mass escape speed in the $a\to0$ limit.

commonErrors.description: Sets the escape energy equal to the local potential rather than zero at infinity.
commonErrors.consequence: The threshold speed has the wrong sign or an extra factor of two.

commonErrors.description: Replaces $\sqrt{r^2+a^2}$ by $r+a$.
commonErrors.consequence: The stated potential model is changed and the numerical escape speed is incorrect.

problems.solution: Marginal escape obeys $0=\tfrac12v_{\mathrm{esc}}^2-\mu/\sqrt{r^2+a^2}$, hence $v_{\mathrm{esc}}=\sqrt{2\mu/\sqrt{r^2+a^2}}$. Here $\sqrt{r^2+a^2}=6.325\times10^6\,\mathrm m$, giving $v_{\mathrm{esc}}=1.12\times10^4\,\mathrm{m/s}$, or $11.2\,\mathrm{km/s}$. When $a\to0$, this becomes $\sqrt{2\mu/r}$.
problems.flawedProof: Escape requires kinetic energy equal to $+\Phi(r)$, so $v_{\mathrm{esc}}^2=2\Phi(r)<0$ and no escape is possible from a softened potential.

problems.title: Reduce a two-body orbit before assigning velocities
problems.objective: Transform a central two-body problem to center-of-mass and relative variables and recover barycentric velocities.
problems.statement: Two particles of masses $m_1=2.00\,\mathrm{kg}$ and $m_2=3.00\,\mathrm{kg}$ interact through a potential $U(|\mathbf r_1-\mathbf r_2|)$. Derive the kinetic-energy split into center-of-mass and relative terms. In the center-of-mass frame, their separation is $5.00\,\mathrm m$ and the relative velocity is perpendicular to the separation with magnitude $4.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Find both particle speeds and the relative angular momentum magnitude.
problems.strategy: Introduce $\mathbf R=(m_1\mathbf r_1+m_2\mathbf r_2)/M$ and $\mathbf r=\mathbf r_1-\mathbf r_2$, invert them, and substitute their time derivatives into the kinetic energy.
hints: $\mathbf r_1=\mathbf R+(m_2/M)\mathbf r$ and $\mathbf r_2=\mathbf R-(m_1/M)\mathbf r$.
In the center-of-mass frame, set $\dot{\mathbf R}=0$ before evaluating speeds.
The relative angular momentum is $\mu_r\,\mathbf r\times\dot{\mathbf r}$.
rubricCriteria: Derives $T=\tfrac12M\dot{\mathbf R}^2+\tfrac12\mu_r\dot{\mathbf r}^2$ with cross terms canceled.
Finds speeds $v_1=2.40\,\mathrm{m/s}$ and $v_2=1.60\,\mathrm{m/s}$ in opposite directions.
Finds relative angular momentum $24.0\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}$ with correct reduced mass and geometry.

commonErrors.description: Uses total mass in the relative kinetic-energy term.
commonErrors.consequence: The transformed kinetic energy and all orbital invariants are too large.

commonErrors.description: Assigns equal and opposite particle speeds despite unequal masses.
commonErrors.consequence: The center of mass would not remain at rest.

problems.solution: With $M=m_1+m_2$ and $\mu_r=m_1m_2/M$, inversion gives $\dot{\mathbf r}_1=\dot{\mathbf R}+(m_2/M)\dot{\mathbf r}$ and $\dot{\mathbf r}_2=\dot{\mathbf R}-(m_1/M)\dot{\mathbf r}$. Substitution cancels the mixed terms and yields $T=\tfrac12M\dot{\mathbf R}^2+\tfrac12\mu_r\dot{\mathbf r}^2$. Here $\mu_r=1.20\,\mathrm{kg}$. With $\dot{\mathbf R}=0$, $v_1=(3/5)(4.00)=2.40\,\mathrm{m/s}$ and $v_2=(2/5)(4.00)=1.60\,\mathrm{m/s}$ oppositely directed. Since the relative velocity is transverse, $\ell=\mu_r r v_{\mathrm{rel}}=(1.20)(5.00)(4.00)=24.0\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}$.
problems.flawedProof: The relative particle has mass $m_1+m_2=5.00\,\mathrm{kg}$. Each real particle therefore moves at half the relative speed, and the orbital angular momentum is $(5.00)(5.00)(4.00)=100\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}$.

problems.title: Conic parameters determine both apsides and period
problems.objective: Convert a Kepler orbit's semilatus rectum and eccentricity into geometric and temporal invariants.
problems.statement: A bound orbit in the potential $-m\mu/r$ has polar equation $r=p/(1+e\cos\phi)$, with $p=9.00\times10^6\,\mathrm m$, $e=0.200$, and $\mu=3.986\times10^{14}\,\mathrm{m^3/s^2}$. Find periapsis, apoapsis, semimajor axis, and period. Identify which angle in the given convention is periapsis.
problems.strategy: Evaluate the denominator at $\cos\phi=\pm1$, use $p=a(1-e^2)$, and then apply Kepler's period relation.
permittedResults: For an elliptic Kepler orbit, $p=a(1-e^2)$ and $T=2\pi\sqrt{a^3/\mu}$.
hints: The smallest radius occurs when the denominator is largest.
Use $a=p/(1-e^2)$ rather than averaging rounded apsides.
The period depends on $a$, not directly on $p$.
rubricCriteria: Finds $r_p=7.50\times10^6\,\mathrm m$ and $r_a=1.125\times10^7\,\mathrm m$ with periapsis at $\phi=0$.
Finds $a=9.375\times10^6\,\mathrm m$.
Finds $T\approx9.03\times10^3\,\mathrm s$ and reports a coherent time unit.

commonErrors.description: Interchanges $1+e$ and $1-e$ when labeling apsides.
commonErrors.consequence: Periapsis is mislabeled as the largest radius.

commonErrors.description: Uses $p$ as the semimajor axis in the period formula.
commonErrors.consequence: The period is systematically underestimated for nonzero eccentricity.

problems.solution: At $\phi=0$, $r_p=p/(1+e)=7.50\times10^6\,\mathrm m$. At $\phi=\pi$, $r_a=p/(1-e)=1.125\times10^7\,\mathrm m$. Also $a=p/(1-e^2)=9.375\times10^6\,\mathrm m$. Therefore $T=2\pi\sqrt{a^3/\mu}=9.03\times10^3\,\mathrm s$, about $151\,\mathrm{min}$.
problems.flawedProof: Because $p$ is the average orbital radius, $a=p=9.00\times10^6\,\mathrm m$. Periapsis occurs at $\phi=\pi$ where $1-e$ is smallest.

problems.title: A tangential state vector identifies the occupied apsis
problems.objective: Classify a Kepler orbit from a single perpendicular position-velocity snapshot and reconstruct its apsides.
problems.statement: A satellite is at radius $r=7.00\times10^6\,\mathrm m$ with purely transverse speed $v=8.00\times10^3\,\mathrm{m/s}$ in a Kepler field with $\mu=3.986\times10^{14}\,\mathrm{m^3/s^2}$. Compute its specific energy, specific angular momentum, semimajor axis, eccentricity, and the other apsis. Decide whether the current point is periapsis or apoapsis.
problems.strategy: Compute $\varepsilon$ and $h$ first, infer $a$ and $e$, and compare the transverse speed with local circular speed to label the current turning point.
hints: Purely transverse motion means the snapshot is at an apsis.
Use $h=rv$ and the negative-energy formula for $a$.
A speed above $\sqrt{\mu/r}$ at an apsis identifies periapsis.
rubricCriteria: Computes $\varepsilon=-2.494\times10^7\,\mathrm{J/kg}$ and $h=5.60\times10^{10}\,\mathrm{m^2/s}$.
Finds $a=7.990\times10^6\,\mathrm m$ and $e=0.1239$.
Identifies the current radius as periapsis and the apoapsis as $8.98\times10^6\,\mathrm m$.

commonErrors.description: Uses total energy units while inserting quantities into specific-energy formulas.
commonErrors.consequence: Mass factors become inconsistent and the reconstructed elements have wrong dimensions.

commonErrors.description: Labels every transverse snapshot as apoapsis.
commonErrors.consequence: The local speed relative to circular speed is ignored, reversing the orbit geometry.

problems.solution: $\varepsilon=(8000)^2/2-3.986\times10^{14}/(7.00\times10^6)=-2.494\times10^7\,\mathrm{J/kg}$ and $h=rv=5.60\times10^{10}\,\mathrm{m^2/s}$. Thus $a=-\mu/(2\varepsilon)=7.990\times10^6\,\mathrm m$ and $e=\sqrt{1+2\varepsilon h^2/\mu^2}=0.1239$. Since $8000\,\mathrm{m/s}>\sqrt{\mu/r}=7546\,\mathrm{m/s}$, this apsis is periapsis. The other is $r_a=a(1+e)=8.98\times10^6\,\mathrm m$.
problems.flawedProof: Choose a $1000\,\mathrm{kg}$ satellite and call $E=mv^2/2-\mu/r$ its total energy in joules. Substituting that joule-valued $E$ directly into the specific relation $a=-\mu/(2E)$ gives the semimajor axis.

problems.title: Specular hard-sphere scattering has an isotropic cross section
problems.objective: Derive the impact-parameter map and differential cross section for elastic reflection from a hard sphere, including endpoint and total-area checks.
problems.statement: A point particle scatters elastically from a fixed impenetrable sphere of radius $R$. Outside the sphere the force vanishes, and at contact the velocity reflects specularly from the local tangent plane. Let $b$ be the impact parameter and let $\Theta\in[0,\pi]$ be the angle between the outgoing velocity and the original incoming direction, so $\Theta=\pi$ is head-on backscatter. Derive $b(\Theta)$ and $d\sigma/d\Omega$ for $0<\Theta<\pi$. Integrate over solid angle to recover the total cross section and check both endpoint limits. For $R=0.200\,\mathrm m$ and $\Theta=60.0^\circ$, compute $b$, $d\sigma/d\Omega$, and the total cross section.
problems.strategy: Relate the contact normal to the impact parameter, use the reflection geometry to express the scattering angle, and then transform incident annular area into scattered solid angle with an absolute Jacobian.
permittedResults: For one monotone azimuthally symmetric branch, $d\sigma/d\Omega=(b/\sin\Theta)|db/d\Theta|$.
hints: If $\alpha$ is the angle between the incoming line and the inward contact normal, then $b=R\sin\alpha$ and $\Theta=\pi-2\alpha$.
Eliminate $\alpha$ to obtain a half-angle relation before differentiating with respect to $\Theta$.
Use $d\Omega=2\pi\sin\Theta\,d\Theta$ and check that the apparent factor $1/\sin\Theta$ cancels at both endpoints.
rubricCriteria: Derives $b=R\cos(\Theta/2)$ from the declared specular-reflection geometry and gets both endpoint limits right.
Applies the absolute annulus-to-solid-angle Jacobian to obtain $d\sigma/d\Omega=R^2/4$.
Recovers $\sigma_{\mathrm{tot}}=\pi R^2$ and computes $b=0.173\,\mathrm m$, $d\sigma/d\Omega=0.0100\,\mathrm{m^2/sr}$, and $\sigma_{\mathrm{tot}}=0.126\,\mathrm{m^2}$.

commonErrors.description: Uses the full scattering angle where the reflection geometry requires a half-angle.
commonErrors.consequence: The impact-parameter map fails the head-on or grazing limit and gives a nonconstant cross section.

commonErrors.description: Reads the factor $1/\sin\Theta$ as an endpoint divergence without combining it with the Jacobian numerator.
commonErrors.consequence: A finite hard-sphere cross section is incorrectly replaced by forward and backward singularities.

problems.solution:
Let $\alpha$ be the angle between the incoming line and the inward normal at contact. The contact geometry gives $b=R\sin\alpha$, while specular reflection turns the velocity through $\Theta=\pi-2\alpha$. Hence $b=R\cos(\Theta/2)$ and $|db/d\Theta|=(R/2)\sin(\Theta/2)$. Therefore
$d\sigma/d\Omega=[R\cos(\Theta/2)/\sin\Theta][(R/2)\sin(\Theta/2)]=R^2/4$,
because $\sin\Theta=2\sin(\Theta/2)\cos(\Theta/2)$. The endpoint limits are $b\to R$ as $\Theta\to0$ for grazing incidence and $b\to0$ as $\Theta\to\pi$ for head-on backscatter; the constant limiting density is finite at both ends. Integration gives $\sigma_{\mathrm{tot}}=(R^2/4)\int d\Omega=\pi R^2$, equal to the geometric shadow area. For $R=0.200\,\mathrm m$ and $\Theta=60.0^\circ$, $b=0.200\cos30^\circ=0.173\,\mathrm m$, $d\sigma/d\Omega=0.0100\,\mathrm{m^2/sr}$, and $\sigma_{\mathrm{tot}}=\pi(0.200)^2=0.126\,\mathrm{m^2}$.
problems.flawedProof: Specular reflection makes the impact parameter $b=R\sin\Theta$. Substituting this full-angle relation into the cross-section Jacobian gives the hard-sphere answer, and no endpoint check is needed.

problems.title: Two apsides fix the energy and angular momentum
problems.objective: Reconstruct Kepler invariants and apsidal speeds from measured periapsis and apoapsis radii.
problems.statement: An elliptic orbit has $r_p=8.00\times10^6\,\mathrm m$, $r_a=1.20\times10^7\,\mathrm m$, and $\mu=3.986\times10^{14}\,\mathrm{m^3/s^2}$. Find $a$, $e$, specific energy $\varepsilon$, specific angular momentum $h$, and the speeds at both apsides. Verify angular-momentum conservation numerically.
problems.strategy: Use the sum and difference of apsides for $a$ and $e$, then compute energy and $h$ before dividing by each radius for the transverse speeds.
hints: At either apsis the velocity is transverse, so $v=h/r$.
rubricCriteria: Finds $a=1.00\times10^7\,\mathrm m$, $e=0.200$, and $\varepsilon=-1.993\times10^7\,\mathrm{J/kg}$.
Finds $h=6.186\times10^{10}\,\mathrm{m^2/s}$.
Finds $v_p=7.73\,\mathrm{km/s}$ and $v_a=5.15\,\mathrm{km/s}$ and verifies $r_pv_p=r_av_a$.

commonErrors.description: Sets the semimajor axis equal to $r_p+r_a$.
commonErrors.consequence: Energy, angular momentum, and both speeds are mis-scaled.

commonErrors.description: Uses the same speed at both apsides.
commonErrors.consequence: Angular momentum is not conserved when the radii differ.

problems.solution: $a=(r_p+r_a)/2=1.00\times10^7\,\mathrm m$ and $e=(r_a-r_p)/(r_a+r_p)=0.200$. Thus $\varepsilon=-\mu/(2a)=-1.993\times10^7\,\mathrm{J/kg}$ and $h=\sqrt{\mu a(1-e^2)}=6.186\times10^{10}\,\mathrm{m^2/s}$. Therefore $v_p=h/r_p=7.73\,\mathrm{km/s}$ and $v_a=h/r_a=5.15\,\mathrm{km/s}$; both products $rv$ equal $h$ to rounding.
problems.flawedProof: $a=r_p+r_a=2.00\times10^7\,\mathrm m$. Energy conservation requires equal kinetic energy at both turning points, so $v_p=v_a$.

problems.title: True anomaly does not advance uniformly in time
problems.objective: Convert true anomaly to eccentric anomaly and time of flight on an elliptic Kepler orbit.
problems.statement: An elliptic orbit has $a=1.00\times10^7\,\mathrm m$, $e=0.500$, and $\mu=3.986\times10^{14}\,\mathrm{m^3/s^2}$. The particle passes periapsis at $t=0$. Find the first time it reaches true anomaly $f=90.0^\circ$. Use the eccentric-anomaly relation and report the corresponding radius as a check.
problems.strategy: Convert $f$ to eccentric anomaly $E$, form mean anomaly $M=E-e\sin E$, and divide by mean motion $n=\sqrt{\mu/a^3}$.
rubricCriteria: Finds $E=\pi/3$ and $M=0.614\,\mathrm{rad}$.
Computes $n=6.31\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and $t\approx973\,\mathrm s$.
Checks the result with $r=7.50\times10^6\,\mathrm m$.

commonErrors.description: Sets eccentric anomaly equal to true anomaly for a noncircular orbit.
commonErrors.consequence: The mean anomaly and time of flight are too large.

commonErrors.description: Inserts degrees into $E-e\sin E$.
commonErrors.consequence: The transcendental equation is evaluated with inconsistent angular units.

problems.solution: $\tan(E/2)=\sqrt{(1/2)/(3/2)}=1/\sqrt3$, so $E=\pi/3$. Then $M=E-e\sin E=1.04720-0.500(0.86603)=0.61418\,\mathrm{rad}$. The mean motion is $n=\sqrt{\mu/a^3}=6.313\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, hence $t=M/n=973\,\mathrm s$. The radius check is $a(1-e\cos E)=a(1-0.25)=7.50\times10^6\,\mathrm m$.
problems.flawedProof: The true anomaly grows at the mean motion, so $t=(\pi/2)/\sqrt{\mu/a^3}=2488\,\mathrm s$. Eccentricity affects only the radius.

problems.title: A pseudo-Newtonian center develops a marginal circular orbit
problems.objective: Use circular and epicyclic frequencies to locate marginal stability in a shifted inverse-radius potential.
problems.statement: For $r>b>0$, a particle moves in the potential per unit mass $\Phi(r)=-\mu/(r-b)$. Derive the circular angular frequency $\Omega(r)$, specific angular momentum $h_c(r)$, and radial epicyclic frequency $\kappa(r)$. Determine the stable circular-orbit range and the marginal radius. At $r=4b$, find $\kappa/\Omega$, the near-circular apsidal angle, and the circular specific energy. Check the limit $b\to0$ at fixed $r$.
problems.strategy: Differentiate the potential for circular balance, differentiate $r^4\Omega^2$ for the epicyclic frequency, and use its sign rather than orbital existence alone to decide stability.
hints: A circular orbit is radially stable only where $\kappa^2>0$.
rubricCriteria: Derives $\Omega^2=\mu/[r(r-b)^2]$, $h_c^2=\mu r^3/(r-b)^2$, and $\kappa^2=\mu(r-3b)/[r(r-b)^3]$.
Identifies $r=3b$ as marginal and $r>3b$ as the stable circular range.
At $r=4b$, obtains $\kappa/\Omega=1/\sqrt3$, apsidal angle $2\pi\sqrt3$, and specific energy $-\mu/(9b)$, with the Kepler limit checked.

commonErrors.description: Uses $\Omega^2>0$ alone as the circular-orbit stability condition.
commonErrors.consequence: Existing but radially unstable circular orbits between $b$ and $3b$ are mislabeled stable.

commonErrors.description: Differentiates after setting $r=4b$ as though the pointwise relation held for all radii.
commonErrors.consequence: The epicyclic derivative and frequency ratio are corrupted.

problems.solution: $\Phi'=\mu/(r-b)^2$, so $\Omega^2=\mu/[r(r-b)^2]$ and $h_c^2=r^4\Omega^2=\mu r^3/(r-b)^2$. Differentiation gives $\kappa^2=\mu(r-3b)/[r(r-b)^3]$. Thus the marginal orbit is $r=3b$, with stability only for $r>3b$. At $r=4b$, $\kappa^2/\Omega^2=(r-3b)/(r-b)=1/3$, so $\kappa/\Omega=1/\sqrt3$ and the pericenter-to-pericenter angle is $2\pi\Omega/\kappa=2\pi\sqrt3$. The circular energy is $\varepsilon=r^2\Omega^2/2+\Phi=\mu(b-r/2)/(r-b)^2=-\mu/(9b)$. As $b\to0$, $\Omega^2=\kappa^2=\mu/r^3$.
problems.flawedProof: Every radius $r>b$ is stable because the circular angular frequency is real. Therefore $\kappa=\Omega$ and the shifted potential has no marginal orbit.

problems.title: Angular momentum raises the repulsive closest approach
problems.objective: Compute the closest approach in repulsive inverse-square scattering from asymptotic energy and impact parameter.
problems.statement: A $1.00\,\mathrm{kg}$ particle approaches from infinity with speed $v_\infty=4.00\,\mathrm{m/s}$ and impact parameter $b=2.00\,\mathrm m$ in the repulsive potential $U(r)=\kappa/r$, $\kappa=8.00\,\mathrm{J\,m}$. Find $E$, $\ell$, and the positive closest-approach radius. Compare it with the head-on value and explain the inequality.
problems.strategy: Evaluate conserved quantities at infinity, set radial kinetic energy to zero at closest approach, and solve the resulting quadratic in $r$.
hints: For a head-on approach set $b=0$ before solving.
rubricCriteria: Computes the asymptotic energy and angular momentum with correct units.
Solves $r^2-r-4=0$ to obtain $r_{\min}=(1+\sqrt{17})/2=2.56\,\mathrm m$.
Finds the head-on value $1.00\,\mathrm m$ and attributes the larger off-axis distance to the centrifugal barrier.

commonErrors.description: Uses $\ell=mv_\infty/r$ instead of $mv_\infty b$.
commonErrors.consequence: Angular momentum has wrong dimensions and cannot be evaluated at infinity.

commonErrors.description: Drops the $\ell^2/(2mr^2)$ term at closest approach.
commonErrors.consequence: Every impact parameter is incorrectly assigned the head-on turning radius.

problems.solution: $E=\tfrac12(1.00)(4.00)^2=8.00\,\mathrm J$ and $\ell=(1.00)(4.00)(2.00)=8.00\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}$. Thus $8.00=8.00/r+32.0/r^2$, or $r^2-r-4=0$. The positive root is $r_{\min}=(1+\sqrt{17})/2=2.56\,\mathrm m$. Head-on, $\ell=0$ and $r_{\min}=\kappa/E=1.00\,\mathrm m$; nonzero angular momentum adds a repulsive effective barrier.
problems.flawedProof: At radius $r$, angular momentum is $\ell=mv_\infty/r$. Insert this expression into the turning-point energy equation and solve for $r$; the impact parameter is unnecessary.

problems.title: Screening changes the circular-speed law
problems.objective: Differentiate a Yukawa-screened potential and derive its circular speed with a controlled unscreened limit.
problems.statement: The potential per unit mass is $\Phi(r)=-\mu e^{-r/a}/r$, where $\mu,a>0$. Derive the radial acceleration and circular speed. Evaluate $v_c$ for $\mu=1.00\times10^5\,\mathrm{m^3/s^2}$, $a=100\,\mathrm m$, and $r=50.0\,\mathrm m$. Check $a\to\infty$ at fixed $r$.
problems.strategy: Use the product rule on $e^{-r/a}/r$, set inward acceleration equal to $v_c^2/r$, and then take the large-screening-length limit.
permittedResults: For a potential per unit mass $\Phi$, $\mathbf a=-\nabla\Phi$.
rubricCriteria: Derives $\mathbf a=-\mu e^{-r/a}(r^{-2}+a^{-1}r^{-1})\hat{\mathbf r}$.
Derives $v_c^2=\mu e^{-r/a}(1/r+1/a)$ and computes $v_c=42.7\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
Recovers $v_c^2=\mu/r$ in the unscreened limit.

commonErrors.description: Differentiates only $1/r$ and treats the exponential as constant.
commonErrors.consequence: The screening-gradient contribution $1/(ar)$ is omitted.

commonErrors.description: Takes $a\to0$ as the unscreened limit.
commonErrors.consequence: The potential instead vanishes at every fixed positive radius.

problems.solution: $d\Phi/dr=\mu e^{-r/a}(1/r^2+1/(ar))$, so $\mathbf a=-\mu e^{-r/a}(1/r^2+1/(ar))\hat{\mathbf r}$. Circular balance gives $v_c^2=\mu e^{-r/a}(1/r+1/a)$. Numerically, $v_c^2=(10^5)e^{-0.5}(0.0200+0.0100)=1.820\times10^3\,\mathrm{m^2/s^2}$, hence $v_c=42.7\,\mathrm{m/s}$. As $a\to\infty$, $v_c^2\to\mu/r$.
problems.flawedProof: The derivative of the exponential cancels the derivative of $1/r$, so the circular speed is zero at $r=a/2$.

problems.title: Epicycles diagnose precession in a softened potential
problems.objective: Derive circular and radial epicyclic frequencies for a softened central potential and convert their ratio into an apsidal angle.
problems.statement: For the potential per unit mass $\Phi(r)=-\mu/(r+a)$ with $a>0$, derive the circular angular frequency $\Omega$ and the small-radial-oscillation frequency $\kappa$ about radius $r_c$. Use $\kappa^2=r^{-3}d(r^4\Omega^2)/dr$. At $r_c=a$, find $\kappa/\Omega$ and the azimuthal angle between successive pericenters. State whether the circular orbit is linearly stable.
problems.strategy: Obtain $\Omega$ from circular balance, differentiate $r^4\Omega^2$ without canceling radius factors early, and compare the radial period with azimuthal advance.
hints: Positive $\kappa^2$ is the linear radial-stability condition.
rubricCriteria: Derives $\Omega^2=\mu/[r(r+a)^2]$ and $\kappa^2=\mu(r+3a)/[r(r+a)^3]$.
Finds $\kappa/\Omega=\sqrt2$ and $\Delta\phi_{\mathrm{peri}}=\sqrt2\pi$ at $r=a$.
Uses $\kappa^2>0$ for $r,a>0$ to establish linear radial stability.

commonErrors.description: Uses $\Omega^2=d\Phi/dr$ without the factor $1/r$.
commonErrors.consequence: The angular frequency has wrong dimensions.

commonErrors.description: Calls $2\pi\kappa/\Omega$ the apsidal angle.
commonErrors.consequence: The frequency ratio is inverted and the predicted precession is wrong.

problems.solution: Circular balance gives $\Omega^2=(1/r)d\Phi/dr=\mu/[r(r+a)^2]$. Since $r^4\Omega^2=\mu r^3/(r+a)^2$, differentiation yields $\kappa^2=\mu(r+3a)/[r(r+a)^3]$. Thus $\kappa^2/\Omega^2=(r+3a)/(r+a)$; at $r=a$, $\kappa/\Omega=\sqrt2$. One radial period advances azimuth by $2\pi\Omega/\kappa=\sqrt2\pi$. Because $\kappa^2>0$ for positive $r$ and $a$, the circular orbit is linearly stable.
problems.flawedProof: Circular balance gives $\Omega^2=d\Phi/dr=\mu/(r+a)^2$. Substitution of this expression into the epicyclic formula gives the two frequencies without any additional factor of $r$.

problems.title: An apsidal measurement reveals a power-law central field
problems.objective: Infer a circular-speed exponent from a measured apsidal angle, then reconstruct and stability-audit the associated power-law effective potential.
problems.statement: A unit test mass moves in an unknown differentiable central potential $\Phi(r)$. Its circular-speed family is known to have the form $v_c(r)=v_*(r/r_*)^\beta$, but the exponent $\beta$ is unknown. A small radial perturbation of the circular orbit at $r_*$ has successive pericenters separated by physical azimuth $\Delta\phi=4\pi/3$. Starting from the fixed-angular-momentum effective potential, derive $\kappa/\Omega$ and the linear stability condition for general $\beta$, infer $\beta$, and reconstruct $\Phi(r)-\Phi(r_*)$. For $v_*=200\,\mathrm{km/s}$, compute $\Phi(2r_*)-\Phi(r_*)$ in $\mathrm{km^2/s^2}$ and $\mathrm{J/kg}$. State the radial acceleration power law and recover the logarithmic-potential limit as $\beta\to0$.
problems.strategy: Build the fixed-angular-momentum curvature at the observed circle, convert its radial-to-azimuthal frequency ratio into the measured pericenter spacing, and only then integrate circular balance to reconstruct the potential.
permittedResults: For a fixed-angular-momentum radial perturbation, $\kappa^2=r^{-3}d(r^4\Omega^2)/dr$ and $\Delta\phi=2\pi\Omega/\kappa$.
rubricCriteria: Derives $\kappa^2=(2\beta+2)\Omega^2$, stability condition $\beta>-1$, and the correct apsidal relation $\Delta\phi=2\pi/\sqrt{2\beta+2}$.
Infers $\beta=1/8$ and obtains $\Phi(r)-\Phi(r_*)=4v_*^2[(r/r_*)^{1/4}-1]$ with inward acceleration proportional to $r^{-3/4}$.
Computes $\Phi(2r_*)-\Phi(r_*)=3.03\times10^4\,\mathrm{km^2/s^2}=3.03\times10^{10}\,\mathrm{J/kg}$ and recovers $v_*^2\ln(r/r_*)$ as $\beta\to0$.

commonErrors.description: Inverts the radial-to-azimuthal frequency ratio when translating the measured pericenter spacing.
commonErrors.consequence: The inferred exponent and reconstructed central-force law are both wrong even if the curvature algebra is otherwise correct.

commonErrors.description: Integrates $v_c^2$ rather than the circular-balance derivative $v_c^2/r$.
commonErrors.consequence: The reconstructed potential has the wrong radius power and fails dimensional and logarithmic-limit checks.

problems.solution: At a circular radius $r_c$ with fixed specific angular momentum $h=r_cv_c$, the effective potential is $\Phi_{\mathrm{eff}}=\Phi+h^2/(2r^2)$. Since $\Phi'=v_c^2/r$ and $v_c\propto r^\beta$, $\Phi''=(2\beta-1)v_c^2/r^2$. Thus $\kappa^2=\Phi_{\mathrm{eff}}''=(2\beta+2)v_c^2/r^2=(2\beta+2)\Omega^2$. Linear stability requires $\beta>-1$, and successive pericenters are separated by $\Delta\phi=2\pi\Omega/\kappa=2\pi/\sqrt{2\beta+2}$. Setting this equal to $4\pi/3$ gives $\sqrt{2\beta+2}=3/2$, hence $\beta=1/8$. Circular balance then gives $\Phi'=v_*^2r^{-1}(r/r_*)^{1/4}$, so $\Phi(r)-\Phi(r_*)=4v_*^2[(r/r_*)^{1/4}-1]$. The acceleration is $\mathbf a=-\Phi'\hat{\mathbf r}$ and scales inward as $r^{-3/4}$. At $r=2r_*$ with $v_*=200\,\mathrm{km/s}$, the potential rise is $4(200)^2(2^{1/4}-1)=3.027\times10^4\,\mathrm{km^2/s^2}=3.027\times10^{10}\,\mathrm{J/kg}$. More generally $\Phi-\Phi(r_*)=[v_*^2/(2\beta)][(r/r_*)^{2\beta}-1]$, whose $\beta\to0$ limit is $v_*^2\ln(r/r_*)$.
problems.flawedProof: The measured fraction $\Delta\phi/(2\pi)$ equals $\kappa/\Omega$. Thus $\kappa/\Omega=2/3$, so $2\beta+2=4/9$ and the inferred exponent is $\beta=-7/9$.

problems.title: The Kepler virial theorem fixes mean energies
problems.objective: Derive the time-averaged virial relation for a bound inverse-square orbit and use it to compute mean kinetic and potential energies.
problems.statement: For a bound orbit in $U(r)=-k/r$, use $G=\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf r$ to derive the time-averaged virial theorem without assuming a circular orbit. Express $\langle T\rangle$ and $\langle U\rangle$ in terms of total energy $E$ and semimajor axis $a$. For a unit mass with $\mu=k/m=3.986\times10^{14}\,\mathrm{m^3/s^2}$ and $a=1.00\times10^7\,\mathrm m$, compute the mean specific kinetic and potential energies.
problems.strategy: Differentiate the bounded virial $G$, average its total derivative over many periods, and use the homogeneity of the inverse-radius potential.
hints: A bounded periodic $G$ has zero long-time average derivative.
rubricCriteria: Derives $2\langle T\rangle+\langle U\rangle=0$ from a bounded total derivative.
Obtains $\langle T\rangle=-E=k/(2a)$ and $\langle U\rangle=2E=-k/a$.
Computes mean specific values $1.993\times10^7\,\mathrm{J/kg}$ and $-3.986\times10^7\,\mathrm{J/kg}$.

commonErrors.description: Sets the instantaneous derivative of $G$ to zero rather than its period average.
commonErrors.consequence: A time-averaged theorem is incorrectly asserted at every orbital point.

commonErrors.description: Uses $\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf F=-U$ for $U=-k/r$.
commonErrors.consequence: The virial signs reverse and predict negative mean kinetic energy.

problems.solution: $\dot G=\dot{\mathbf p}\cdot\mathbf r+\mathbf p\cdot\dot{\mathbf r}=\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf r+2T$. For $U=-k/r$, $\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf F=-k/r=U$. A bound periodic orbit has $\langle\dot G\rangle=0$, so $2\langle T\rangle+\langle U\rangle=0$. Therefore $E=\langle T\rangle+\langle U\rangle=-\langle T\rangle=\langle U\rangle/2$, giving $\langle T\rangle=k/(2a)$ and $\langle U\rangle=-k/a$. Per unit mass, the stated data give $\langle T\rangle/m=1.993\times10^7\,\mathrm{J/kg}$ and $\langle U\rangle/m=-3.986\times10^7\,\mathrm{J/kg}$.
problems.flawedProof: $G$ is conserved in any central force, so $0=2T+U$ at every instant. Hence an eccentric orbit has constant speed.

problems.title: An inverse-square correction produces exact apsidal precession
problems.objective: Solve the orbit equation for a Kepler potential with an additional inverse-square potential term and determine the signed apsidal precession.
problems.statement: A particle of mass $m$ and specific angular momentum $h$ moves in $U(r)=-k/r+\alpha/r^2$, with $k>0$ and $1+2\alpha/(mh^2)>0$. Derive and solve Binet's equation. Find the angle between successive pericenters and its excess over $2\pi$. Evaluate the excess when $\alpha/(mh^2)=0.0100$, and state whether it is prograde or retrograde.
problems.strategy: Differentiate the full potential to get the radial force, insert it into Binet's equation, and read the apsidal interval from the frequency of the cosine in $u(\phi)$.
hints: Collect the term proportional to $u$ on the left and define $\nu^2=1+2\alpha/(mh^2)$.
Successive radial maxima of $u$ are separated by $2\pi/\nu$.
rubricCriteria: Derives $u''+\nu^2u=k/(mh^2)$ with $\nu^2=1+2\alpha/(mh^2)$.
Obtains $u=u_c[1+e\cos(\nu(\phi-\phi_0))]$ and $\Delta\phi=2\pi/\nu$.
Computes an excess of $-0.0619\,\mathrm{rad}$ per radial cycle and correctly identifies retrograde precession.

commonErrors.description: Differentiates $\alpha/r^2$ with the wrong sign.
commonErrors.consequence: The precession frequency shifts in the opposite direction.

commonErrors.description: Calls $2\pi(\nu-1)$ the apsidal excess.
commonErrors.consequence: The angular interval is inverted and even its small-correction magnitude is wrong.

problems.solution:
$F=-dU/dr=-k/r^2+2\alpha/r^3$. Binet's equation gives $u''+u=k/(mh^2)-2\alpha u/(mh^2)$, hence $u''+
u^2u=k/(mh^2)$ with $
u=\sqrt{1+2\alpha/(mh^2)}$. Thus $u=k/(mh^2
u^2)+A\cos[
u(\phi-\phi_0)]$, equivalently a constant times $1+e\cos[
u(\phi-\phi_0)]$. Pericenters are separated by $\Delta\phi=2\pi/
u$, so the signed excess is $2\pi(1/
u-1)$. For $\alpha/(mh^2)=0.0100$, $
u=\sqrt{1.02}$ and the excess is $-0.0619\,\mathrm{rad}=-3.55^\circ$, retrograde.
problems.flawedProof: Since $d(\alpha/r^2)/dr=+2\alpha/r^3$, the correction to the force is $-2\alpha/r^3$. Binet's equation therefore has $\nu^2=1-2\alpha/(mh^2)$.

problems.title: A resonant Binet correction advances the periapsis
problems.objective: Extract the leading secular periapsis advance from a weak nonlinear correction to the Kepler orbit equation.
problems.statement: Consider the corrected orbit equation $u''+u=\mu/h^2+3\mu u^2/c^2$. Treat the last term to first order in $\mu/(c^2p)$, where $p=h^2/\mu=a(1-e^2)$. Starting from $u_0=(1/p)(1+e\cos\phi)$, isolate the resonant term and derive the leading periapsis advance per revolution. Evaluate it for $\mu=1.327\times10^{20}\,\mathrm{m^3/s^2}$, $a=1.00\times10^{10}\,\mathrm m$, $e=0.200$, and $c=3.00\times10^8\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
problems.strategy: Substitute the Kepler solution only on the perturbing right side, retain the cosine term that resonates with the homogeneous equation, and reinterpret the secular $\phi\sin\phi$ term as a shifted orbital frequency.
permittedResults: For $y''+y=C\cos\phi$, a resonant particular solution is $(C/2)\phi\sin\phi$.
hints: The term in $3\mu u_0^2/c^2$ proportional to $\cos\phi$ has coefficient $6\mu e/(c^2p^2)$.
Use $p=a(1-e^2)$ only after deriving the symbolic shift.
rubricCriteria: Identifies the resonant forcing and obtains the secular correction $3\mu e\phi\sin\phi/(c^2p^2)$.
Derives $\Delta\varpi=6\pi\mu/[c^2a(1-e^2)]$ per orbit with a positive sign.
Computes $\Delta\varpi=2.90\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{rad}$ per orbit and states the perturbative smallness condition.

commonErrors.description: Retains only the constant part of $u_0^2$ and discards the resonant cosine.
commonErrors.consequence: The secular frequency shift and periapsis advance disappear.

commonErrors.description: Uses $a$ instead of $p=a(1-e^2)$ in the derivation.
commonErrors.consequence: The eccentricity dependence of the precession is lost.

problems.solution: Using $u_0=(1+e\cos\phi)/p$, the perturbation contains a resonant term $[6\mu e/(c^2p^2)]\cos\phi$. Therefore $\delta u_{\mathrm{sec}}=[3\mu e/(c^2p^2)]\phi\sin\phi$. Writing $(e/p)\cos[(1-\delta)\phi]\simeq(e/p)(\cos\phi+\delta\phi\sin\phi)$ gives $\delta=3\mu/(c^2p)$. One radial cycle then advances by $2\pi/(1-\delta)\simeq2\pi+2\pi\delta$, so $\Delta\varpi=6\pi\mu/(c^2p)=6\pi\mu/[c^2a(1-e^2)]$. The data give $2.90\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{rad}$ per orbit. The result requires $\mu/(c^2p)\ll1$.
problems.flawedProof: Because the correction is proportional to $u^2$, it only changes the eccentricity. Replacing $u^2$ by its average proves there is no periapsis shift.

problems.title: Kepler attraction plus harmonic confinement has two orbital clocks
problems.objective: Compute circular and epicyclic frequencies in a composite central potential and test stability at a calibrated radius.
problems.statement: For the potential per unit mass $\Phi(r)=-\mu/r+\tfrac12\omega_0^2r^2$, derive the circular frequency $\Omega(r)$ and radial epicyclic frequency $\kappa(r)$. At a radius $r_c$ satisfying $\mu/r_c^3=\omega_0^2$, find $\kappa/\Omega$ and the near-circular apsidal angle. Check both limits $\omega_0\to0$ and $\mu\to0$.
problems.strategy: Differentiate the composite potential, use circular balance for $\Omega$, evaluate $r^{-3}d(r^4\Omega^2)/dr$, and only then impose the calibrated-radius relation.
hints: The apsidal angle is $2\pi\Omega/\kappa$, not its reciprocal.
rubricCriteria: Derives $\Omega^2=\mu/r^3+\omega_0^2$ and $\kappa^2=\mu/r^3+4\omega_0^2$.
At the calibrated radius, obtains $\kappa/\Omega=\sqrt{5/2}$ and $\Delta\phi=2\pi\sqrt{2/5}$.
Recovers equal frequencies in the Kepler limit and $\kappa=2\Omega$ in the pure isotropic-oscillator limit.

commonErrors.description: Adds the potential terms but subtracts their positive frequency contributions.
commonErrors.consequence: A manifestly confining term is made spuriously destabilizing.

commonErrors.description: Imposes $\mu/r_c^3=\omega_0^2$ before differentiating with respect to radius.
commonErrors.consequence: A relation valid at one radius is incorrectly treated as a functional identity.

problems.solution: $d\Phi/dr=\mu/r^2+\omega_0^2r$, so $\Omega^2=\mu/r^3+\omega_0^2$. Then $r^4\Omega^2=\mu r+\omega_0^2r^4$, giving $\kappa^2=\mu/r^3+4\omega_0^2>0$. At $\mu/r_c^3=\omega_0^2$, $\Omega^2=2\omega_0^2$ and $\kappa^2=5\omega_0^2$, so $\kappa/\Omega=\sqrt{5/2}$ and $\Delta\phi=2\pi\sqrt{2/5}$. If $\omega_0\to0$, $\kappa=\Omega$; if $\mu\to0$, $\kappa=2\Omega$, as required for the isotropic oscillator.
problems.flawedProof: The two potentials add in $\Omega^2$, but their radial-frequency effects oppose: $\kappa^2=\mu/r^3-4\omega_0^2$. At the stated radius this is negative, so the circular orbit is unstable.

problems.title: Newton iteration solves a high-eccentricity orbital timestamp
problems.objective: Solve Kepler's equation reproducibly and convert the root into radius and true anomaly.
problems.statement: An elliptic orbit has eccentricity $e=0.600$ and mean anomaly $M=1.000\,\mathrm{rad}$. Starting from $E_0=M$, write Newton's update for $E-e\sin E=M$ and iterate until the residual magnitude is below $10^{-10}$. Report $E$, $r/a$, and true anomaly $f$ in radians. Include a residual check and choose the branch continuous from periapsis.
problems.strategy: Apply Newton's method to the explicitly defined scalar residual, verify the converged residual, and then use standard eccentric-to-true-anomaly relations with a quadrant-aware function.
hints: The converged root lies between $1$ and $2$ radians.
Use $\operatorname{atan2}$ to avoid selecting the wrong true-anomaly quadrant.
rubricCriteria: States and correctly applies Newton's update from $E_0=1.000$.
Obtains $E=1.5997485482$ with residual below $10^{-10}$.
Computes $r/a=1.0173689061$ and $f=2.2372603508\,\mathrm{rad}$ on the correct branch.

commonErrors.description: Uses derivative $1+e\cos E$ in Newton's denominator.
commonErrors.consequence: The iteration targets the wrong local linearization and may converge slowly or incorrectly.

commonErrors.description: Uses a one-argument arctangent for $f$ without a quadrant check.
commonErrors.consequence: The returned true anomaly can differ by $\pi$ from the physical branch.

problems.solution: For $F(E)=E-0.600\sin E-1.000$, Newton's method is $E_{n+1}=E_n-F(E_n)/(1-0.600\cos E_n)$. From $E_0=1.000$, it converges to $E=1.5997485482$; substituting gives residual below $10^{-12}$. Then $r/a=1-0.600\cos E=1.0173689061$. The quadrant-aware anomaly formula gives $f=2.2372603508\,\mathrm{rad}$, continuous from $f=0$ at periapsis.
problems.flawedProof: Newton's update is $E_{n+1}=E_n-[E_n-e\sin E_n-M]/[1+e\cos E_n]$. Starting at $E_0=M$ and iterating this denominator gives the required anomaly.

problems.title: Hyperbolic excess data fix a flyby geometry
problems.objective: Reconstruct a Kepler hyperbola from excess speed and periapsis and compute its impact parameter and deflection.
problems.statement: A spacecraft approaches a body with $\mu=398600\,\mathrm{km^3/s^2}$, hyperbolic excess speed $v_\infty=10.0\,\mathrm{km/s}$, and periapsis radius $r_p=7000\,\mathrm{km}$. Find the signed semimajor axis, eccentricity, impact parameter, deflection angle, and periapsis speed. Check energy and angular momentum at infinity and periapsis.
problems.strategy: Use positive hyperbolic energy to obtain $a<0$, express periapsis in terms of $|a|$ and $e$, then use $b=|a|\sqrt{e^2-1}$ and vis-viva.
rubricCriteria: Finds $a=-3986\,\mathrm{km}$ and $e=2.756$.
Finds $b=1.024\times10^4\,\mathrm{km}$ and $\delta=0.743\,\mathrm{rad}=42.5^\circ$.
Finds $v_p=14.62\,\mathrm{km/s}$ and verifies both specific energy and angular momentum.

commonErrors.description: Uses a positive semimajor axis with positive hyperbolic energy.
commonErrors.consequence: The conic is misclassified as an ellipse and the periapsis relation changes sign.

commonErrors.description: Equates the impact parameter with periapsis radius.
commonErrors.consequence: Gravitational bending and angular-momentum conservation are ignored.

problems.solution: $a=-\mu/v_\infty^2=-3986\,\mathrm{km}$ and $e=1+r_p/|a|=2.756$. Thus $b=|a|\sqrt{e^2-1}=1.024\times10^4\,\mathrm{km}$ and $\delta=2\arcsin(1/e)=0.7426\,\mathrm{rad}=42.5^\circ$. Energy gives $v_p=\sqrt{v_\infty^2+2\mu/r_p}=14.62\,\mathrm{km/s}$. The angular-momentum check is $bv_\infty=r_pv_p\approx1.024\times10^5\,\mathrm{km^2/s}$; both points also give specific energy $v_\infty^2/2=50.0\,\mathrm{km^2/s^2}$.
problems.flawedProof: Positive specific energy requires a positive semimajor axis, so $a=+\mu/v_\infty^2=3986\,\mathrm{km}$. Use this positive $a$ in the hyperbola formulas for $e$ and $b$.

problems.title: A tangential burn at periapsis sets the opposite apsis
problems.objective: Propagate an instantaneous velocity change into new Kepler elements and verify the occupied apsis.
problems.statement: A spacecraft initially follows a circular orbit of radius $8000\,\mathrm{km}$ around a body with $\mu=398600\,\mathrm{km^3/s^2}$. It receives an instantaneous $0.500\,\mathrm{km/s}$ prograde tangential burn. Find the new specific energy, semimajor axis, eccentricity, apoapsis radius, and period. Prove that the burn point is periapsis rather than assuming it.
problems.strategy: Add the burn to the circular speed, recompute energy and angular momentum at fixed position, and infer the apsis label from the radial velocity and speed relative to circular.
hints: Immediately after a tangential burn, radial speed remains zero.
A speed above the local circular value at an apsis identifies periapsis.
rubricCriteria: Computes postburn speed $7.559\,\mathrm{km/s}$ and specific energy $-21.26\,\mathrm{km^2/s^2}$.
Finds $a=9375\,\mathrm{km}$, $e=0.1467$, and $r_a=10750\,\mathrm{km}$.
Finds $T=9034\,\mathrm s$ and justifies the burn point as periapsis from the zero radial speed and supercircular tangential speed.

commonErrors.description: Adds $0.500\,\mathrm{km^2/s^2}$ to energy instead of adding the velocity before squaring.
commonErrors.consequence: The burn's kinetic cross term is omitted.

commonErrors.description: Treats the burn point as apoapsis because it is the only known radius.
commonErrors.consequence: The eccentricity and opposite apsis are reversed.

problems.solution: $v_c=\sqrt{398600/8000}=7.059\,\mathrm{km/s}$, so $v=7.559\,\mathrm{km/s}$ and $\varepsilon=v^2/2-\mu/r=-21.26\,\mathrm{km^2/s^2}$. Thus $a=-\mu/(2\varepsilon)=9375\,\mathrm{km}$. The radial speed is zero and $v>v_c$, so the point is periapsis: $e=1-r_p/a=0.1467$. Hence $r_a=a(1+e)=10750\,\mathrm{km}$ and $T=2\pi\sqrt{a^3/\mu}=9034\,\mathrm s$.
problems.flawedProof: The new energy is the old energy plus $0.500$, so the orbit remains almost circular. Since the burn occurs first, that point must be apoapsis.

problems.title: Slow central-mass growth preserves Kepler eccentricity
problems.objective: Combine exact angular-momentum conservation with radial action invariance to scale a Kepler ellipse under slow parameter change.
problems.statement: A bound test particle moves in $\Phi(r,t)=-\mu(t)/r$, where the central parameter changes isotropically on a timescale much longer than the orbital period. Assume no separatrix crossing. Use exact angular-momentum conservation and adiabatic invariance of the radial action to derive how semimajor axis $a$, eccentricity $e$, specific energy $\varepsilon$, and period $T$ scale with $\mu$. If $\mu$ slowly doubles from an initial ellipse $(a_i,e_i)$, find $a_f/a_i$, $e_f$, $\varepsilon_f/\varepsilon_i$, and $T_f/T_i$. Contrast the conclusion with an instantaneous parameter jump.
problems.strategy: Use centrality for exact $h$, combine $J_r=\sqrt{\mu a}-h$ with adiabatic invariance, and then propagate the invariant product $\mu a$ through the standard Kepler element relations.
permittedResults: For a bound Kepler orbit, $J_r=\sqrt{\mu a}-h$, $h^2=\mu a(1-e^2)$, and $T=2\pi\sqrt{a^3/\mu}$.
hints: The force remains radial even while $\mu(t)$ changes, so $h$ is exactly constant.
Adiabatic $J_r$ and exact $h$ together make $\sqrt{\mu a}$ constant.
Use the constant product $\mu a$ in both $h^2=\mu a(1-e^2)$ and the period formula.
rubricCriteria: Shows $h$ is exactly conserved and $\mu a$ is adiabatically constant.
Derives $e=\mathrm{constant}$, $a\propto\mu^{-1}$, $\varepsilon\propto-\mu^2$, and $T\propto\mu^{-2}$.
For doubled $\mu$, reports $a_f/a_i=1/2$, $e_f=e_i$, $\varepsilon_f/\varepsilon_i=4$, and $T_f/T_i=1/4$, while stating the slow-change limitation.

commonErrors.description: Assumes energy is conserved despite explicit time dependence of $\mu(t)$.
commonErrors.consequence: The orbit fails to contract and the work done by the changing central field is omitted.

commonErrors.description: Applies adiabatic action invariance to an instantaneous jump.
commonErrors.consequence: The timescale hypothesis is violated; eccentricity can change under a sudden parameter change.

problems.solution: Because the force is radial at every time, $h$ is exactly conserved. Slow evolution also preserves $J_r=\sqrt{\mu a}-h$, so $J_r+h=\sqrt{\mu a}$ and therefore $\mu a$ are constant. Then $h^2=\mu a(1-e^2)$ forces $e$ to remain constant. Hence $a\propto\mu^{-1}$, $\varepsilon=-\mu/(2a)\propto-\mu^2$, and $T=2\pi\sqrt{a^3/\mu}\propto\mu^{-2}$. If $\mu_f=2\mu_i$, then $a_f/a_i=1/2$, $e_f=e_i$, $\varepsilon_f/\varepsilon_i=4$ for the signed negative energies, and $T_f/T_i=1/4$. An instantaneous jump preserves state rather than radial action and generally changes eccentricity.
problems.flawedProof: The force is central, so both angular momentum and energy remain exact constants while $\mu$ changes. Therefore $a$, $e$, and $T$ are all unchanged.

problems.title: The Kepler tidal tensor stretches one way and squeezes two
problems.objective: Linearize inverse-square acceleration between nearby trajectories and interpret the eigenvalues of the tidal tensor.
problems.statement: For $\mathbf a(\mathbf r)=-\mu\mathbf r/r^3$, derive the Jacobian $T_{ij}=\partial a_i/\partial r_j$ and its eigenvalues along one radial and two transverse directions. Explain why its trace vanishes away from the origin. At $r=1.00\times10^7\,\mathrm m$ with $\mu=3.986\times10^{14}\,\mathrm{m^3/s^2}$, find the instantaneous relative acceleration for a $100\,\mathrm m$ separation first radial and then transverse.
problems.strategy: Differentiate the vector field componentwise, project the tensor on radial and transverse unit vectors, and apply $\delta\ddot{\mathbf r}=T\delta\mathbf r$.
permittedResults: To first order, $\mathbf a(\mathbf r+\delta\mathbf r)-\mathbf a(\mathbf r)=T\delta\mathbf r$.
hints: The radial eigenvalue is twice the magnitude and opposite in sign to either transverse eigenvalue.
rubricCriteria: Derives $T_{ij}=(\mu/r^3)(3\hat r_i\hat r_j-\delta_{ij})$.
Finds eigenvalues $2\mu/r^3,-\mu/r^3,-\mu/r^3$ and zero trace.
Computes $+7.97\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ radially and $-3.99\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ transversely for the stated separation.

commonErrors.description: Differentiates only the vector $\mathbf r$ and treats $r^{-3}$ as constant.
commonErrors.consequence: The anisotropic radial stretching term is omitted.

commonErrors.description: Interprets the negative transverse eigenvalues as attraction toward the central origin rather than relative squeezing.
commonErrors.consequence: Absolute acceleration is confused with the differential acceleration between neighboring trajectories.

problems.solution: $a_i=-\mu r_i r^{-3}$ gives $T_{ij}=-\mu(\delta_{ij}r^{-3}-3r_ir_jr^{-5})=(\mu/r^3)(3\hat r_i\hat r_j-\delta_{ij})$. Acting on $\hat{\mathbf r}$ gives $2\mu/r^3$; acting on either transverse vector gives $-\mu/r^3$. Their sum is zero, consistent with $\nabla^2(-\mu/r)=0$ away from the source. Here $\mu/r^3=3.986\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm{s^{-2}}$. Multiplying by $100\,\mathrm m$ gives radial stretching $+7.97\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ and transverse squeezing $-3.99\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
problems.flawedProof: Because both nearby particles accelerate inward, their relative acceleration is zero. The tidal tensor is therefore the zero matrix outside the source.

problems.title: Weak drag shrinks a Kepler circle exponentially
problems.objective: Derive exact energy and angular-momentum loss rates under linear drag and obtain the adiabatic circular inspiral law.
problems.statement: A mass $m$ moves in $U=-m\mu/r$ with an additional weak drag $\mathbf F_d=-\gamma\mathbf v$, where $\gamma$ has units $\mathrm{kg/s}$. Derive exact formulas for $dE/dt$ and $d\mathbf L/dt$. Assuming the orbit remains nearly circular as it slowly shrinks, derive $r(t)$ from $r(0)=r_0$. For $m=100\,\mathrm{kg}$ and $\gamma=0.0100\,\mathrm{kg/s}$, find the e-folding time of the radius and verify consistency with the angular-momentum rate.
problems.strategy: Dot the full equation with velocity for power, cross it with position for torque, and then insert circular Kepler relations only in the slow-evolution step.
permittedResults: For a circular Kepler orbit, $E=-m\mu/(2r)$ and $v^2=\mu/r$.
hints: The central force contributes neither net mechanical power beyond $-dU/dt$ nor torque.
Differentiate $E(r)=-m\mu/(2r)$ and set it equal to $-\gamma\mu/r$.
rubricCriteria: Derives exact rates $\dot E=-\gamma v^2$ and $\dot{\mathbf L}=-(\gamma/m)\mathbf L$.
Obtains $\dot r=-(2\gamma/m)r$ and $r=r_0e^{-2\gamma t/m}$ under the adiabatic circular assumption.
Finds a radius e-folding time of $5000\,\mathrm s$ and checks that $L\propto\sqrt r$ decays at rate $\gamma/m$.

commonErrors.description: Treats mechanical energy as conserved because the central part of the force is conservative.
commonErrors.consequence: The negative drag power is omitted.

commonErrors.description: Uses $L\propto r$ for a circular Kepler orbit.
commonErrors.consequence: The angular-momentum decay conflicts with the derived radius law.

problems.solution: $\dot E=\mathbf F_d\cdot\mathbf v=-\gamma v^2$. Also $\dot{\mathbf L}=\mathbf r\times\mathbf F_d=-\gamma\mathbf r\times\mathbf v=-(\gamma/m)\mathbf L$. For a slowly evolving circle, $\dot E=(m\mu/2r^2)\dot r$ while $-\gamma v^2=-\gamma\mu/r$, so $\dot r=-(2\gamma/m)r$ and $r=r_0e^{-2\gamma t/m}$. The e-folding time is $m/(2\gamma)=5000\,\mathrm s$. Since $L=m\sqrt{\mu r}$, its logarithmic decay rate is half that of $r$, namely $-\gamma/m$, exactly matching the torque equation.
problems.flawedProof: Drag is radial on a circular orbit, so it changes neither energy nor angular momentum. The radius stays fixed while the speed decreases.

problems.title: Linearized Kepler motion in a rotating orbital frame
problems.objective: Derive the planar Hill equations about a circular Kepler orbit and construct their bounded epicyclic solution.
problems.statement: A reference particle follows a circular Kepler orbit of radius $R$ and mean motion $n=\sqrt{\mu/R^3}$. In a frame rotating with that orbit, let $x$ be a small outward displacement and $y$ a small along-track displacement. Linearize the exact rotating-frame equations to derive the planar Hill equations. Then solve them for $x(0)=x_0$, $y(0)=0$, $\dot x(0)=0$, and the unique $\dot y(0)$ that removes secular drift.
problems.strategy: Expand the Kepler field to first order about the reference radius, retain Coriolis and centrifugal terms with declared axes, integrate the along-track equation once, and impose zero integration constant for bounded motion.
permittedResults: In a uniformly rotating frame, $\mathbf a_I=\mathbf a_R+2\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf v_R+\boldsymbol\Omega\times(\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf r)$ for constant $\boldsymbol\Omega$.
hints: The linear planar equations are expected to contain Coriolis coupling and a $-3n^2x$ radial term.
Bounded motion about the same guiding center requires $C=0$.
rubricCriteria: Derives $\ddot x-2n\dot y-3n^2x=0$ and $\ddot y+2n\dot x=0$ with correct signs.
Finds the no-drift condition $\dot y(0)=-2nx_0$.
Obtains $x=x_0\cos nt$ and $y=-2x_0\sin nt$ and verifies both equations and dimensions.

commonErrors.description: Drops the Coriolis terms while retaining the rotating axes.
commonErrors.consequence: The epicyclic solution and drift condition cannot satisfy the frame dynamics.

commonErrors.description: Sets $\dot y(0)=0$ and still claims a closed epicycle about the original guiding center.
commonErrors.consequence: A nonzero integration constant produces secular along-track drift.

problems.solution: First-order expansion of gravity plus centrifugal acceleration about $R$ gives $\ddot x-2n\dot y-3n^2x=0$ and $\ddot y+2n\dot x=0$. The second integrates to $\dot y+2nx=C$. Substitution into the first gives $\ddot x+n^2x=2nC$. To avoid an offset and secular drift about the original guiding center, take $C=0$, requiring $\dot y(0)=-2nx_0$. Then $x=x_0\cos nt$ and integration of $\dot y=-2nx$ with $y(0)=0$ gives $y=-2x_0\sin nt$. Direct substitution verifies both equations.
problems.flawedProof: The rotating frame makes the reference particle stationary, so nearby particles obey $\ddot x=\ddot y=0$. Choosing zero initial relative velocity therefore gives a closed orbit.

problems.title: A scattering rainbow is a Jacobian singularity, not infinite probability
problems.objective: Derive the multibranch classical differential cross section and distinguish rainbow and orbiting singular boundaries.
problems.statement: For azimuthally symmetric central scattering, a deflection angle $\Theta(b)$ can have multiple impact parameters for one observed angle. Derive $d\sigma/d\Omega$ as a sum over branches. Near a rainbow, suppose $\Theta(b)=\Theta_0+\alpha(b-b_0)^2$ with $\alpha>0$. Derive the leading singularity. Then use $b_0=5.00\,\mathrm{km}$, $\Theta_0=60.0^\circ$, $\alpha=0.0200\,\mathrm{rad/km^2}$ to find the branches and $d\sigma/d\Omega$ at $\Theta=60.5^\circ$. Finally contrast this stationary-deflection boundary with orbiting behavior $\Theta(b)\sim-A\ln|b-b_c|+B$.
problems.strategy: Equate incident annular area to scattered solid-angle area branch by branch, invert the quadratic map locally, and reserve a separate branch-summing analysis for logarithmically divergent orbiting angles.
permittedResults: An incident annulus has area $d\sigma=2\pi b\,db$ and an azimuthal scattering ring has $d\Omega=2\pi\sin\Theta\,d\Theta$.
hints: An orbiting logarithm creates many winding branches after angles are identified modulo $2\pi$; it is not a zero-slope quadratic turning point.
rubricCriteria: Derives $d\sigma/d\Omega=\sum_i[b_i/\sin\Theta]|db_i/d\Theta|$ with absolute Jacobians.
Shows the rainbow divergence is proportional to $(\Theta-\Theta_0)^{-1/2}$ and computes branches $4.34$ and $5.66\,\mathrm{km}$ with $d\sigma/d\Omega\approx435\,\mathrm{km^2/sr}$.
Explains that the singular idealization is integrable and distinguishes it from the infinite winding-branch structure near an orbiting threshold.

commonErrors.description: Keeps only one of the two impact-parameter branches near the rainbow.
commonErrors.consequence: The cross section is underestimated and the branch geometry is lost.

commonErrors.description: Treats the divergent density at one angle as an infinite integrated cross section and calls every divergence orbiting.
commonErrors.consequence: An integrable Jacobian caustic is confused with a logarithmic winding boundary.

problems.solution: Branchwise area conservation gives $d\sigma/d\Omega=\sum_i b_i|db_i/d\Theta|/\sin\Theta$. For the quadratic map, $b_\pm=b_0\pm\sqrt{(\Theta-\Theta_0)/\alpha}$ and $|db/d\Theta|=[2\sqrt{\alpha(\Theta-\Theta_0)}]^{-1}$, so the cross section diverges as $(\Theta-\Theta_0)^{-1/2}$ but its angular integral remains finite. Here $\Theta-\Theta_0=0.00872665\,\mathrm{rad}$, giving $b_-=4.339\,\mathrm{km}$ and $b_+=5.661\,\mathrm{km}$. Summing both branches at $\Theta=60.5^\circ$ gives $d\sigma/d\Omega=4.35\times10^2\,\mathrm{km^2/sr}$. In orbiting, $\Theta$ itself diverges logarithmically as $b\to b_c$, so observed angles modulo $2\pi$ receive infinitely many winding branches; that mechanism is distinct from $d\Theta/db=0$ at a rainbow.
problems.flawedProof: The cross section is simply $b^2$ for whichever root is larger. At $d\Theta/db=0$ the total probability is infinite, and the same zero derivative defines orbiting.

problems.title: Unrolling a cone reveals geometric apsidal precession
problems.objective: Solve a Kepler problem constrained to a cone by unrolling its metric and distinguish geometric from force-law precession.
problems.statement: A unit-mass particle is constrained to the surface of a right circular cone with half-angle $0<\beta\le\pi/2$. Let $r$ be slant distance from the apex and $\phi$ the azimuth about the cone axis. The potential is $\Phi(r)=-\mu/r$. Derive the kinetic metric, conserved azimuthal momentum $h$, and orbit equation by defining an unrolled angle $\psi=\sin\beta\,\phi$. Find the angle in physical azimuth between successive pericenters and the semilatus rectum. Evaluate both for $\beta=30.0^\circ$ in terms of $h$ and $\mu$, and check the flat-plane limit.
problems.strategy: Derive the induced cone metric, rescale azimuth to a Euclidean polar angle on the unrolled sector, solve the ordinary Kepler conic there, and map its radial period back to physical azimuth.
permittedResults: A cone parameterized by $(r,\phi)$ has line element $ds^2=dr^2+r^2\sin^2\beta\,d\phi^2$.
hints: With $\psi=\sin\beta\,\phi$, the unrolled specific angular momentum is $j=r^2\dot\psi=h/\sin\beta$.
The Kepler conic repeats after $\Delta\psi=2\pi$, so divide by $\sin\beta$ to recover $\Delta\phi$.
rubricCriteria: Derives the cone Lagrangian, conserved $h$, and unrolled angular momentum $j=h/\sin\beta$.
Obtains $r=p/[1+e\cos(\sin\beta(\phi-\phi_0))]$ with $p=h^2/(\mu\sin^2\beta)$ and $\Delta\phi=2\pi/\sin\beta$.
For $\beta=30^\circ$, reports $p=4h^2/\mu$ and $\Delta\phi=4\pi$, and recovers the planar Kepler orbit as $\beta\to\pi/2$.

commonErrors.description: Treats physical azimuth $\phi$ as the Euclidean polar angle on the unrolled cone.
commonErrors.consequence: The cone metric factor is lost and the geometric precession disappears.

commonErrors.description: Uses $h$ rather than $h/\sin\beta$ as unrolled angular momentum.
commonErrors.consequence: The semilatus rectum has the wrong cone-angle dependence.

problems.solution: The cone metric gives $L=\tfrac12(\dot r^2+r^2\sin^2\beta\,\dot\phi^2)+\mu/r$ and $h=r^2\sin^2\beta\,\dot\phi$. Define $\psi=\sin\beta\,\phi$; then the kinetic term is ordinary polar form and $j=r^2\dot\psi=h/\sin\beta$. The unrolled Kepler solution is $r=p/[1+e\cos(\psi-\psi_0)]$ with $p=j^2/\mu=h^2/(\mu\sin^2\beta)$. Thus physical pericenters are separated by $\Delta\phi=2\pi/\sin\beta$. At $\beta=30^\circ$, $p=4h^2/\mu$ and $\Delta\phi=4\pi$: the particle winds twice around the cone between pericenters. As $\beta\to\pi/2$, $p\to h^2/\mu$ and $\Delta\phi\to2\pi$.
problems.flawedProof: The cone is locally flat, so $\phi$ is already the unrolled polar angle and every Kepler orbit closes after $2\pi$ in physical azimuth.

problems.title: Kepler radial action explains closed bound orbits
problems.objective: Evaluate the radial action of the bound Kepler problem and use action derivatives to recover frequency degeneracy.
problems.statement: Use the specific Hamiltonian $H=\tfrac12(p_r^2+h^2/r^2)-\mu/r=\varepsilon<0$, treating $h>0$ as the azimuthal action. Evaluate $J_r=(2\pi)^{-1}\oint p_r\,dr$ and rewrite $H$ in terms of $J_r+h$. Show that the radial and azimuthal action frequencies are equal. For $\mu=3.986\times10^{14}\,\mathrm{m^3/s^2}$, $a=1.00\times10^7\,\mathrm m$, and $e=0.600$, compute $h$, $J_r$, and the common frequency.
problems.strategy: Express the radial momentum between the two turning points, evaluate the closed action integral using the eccentric-anomaly substitution, then differentiate the resulting Hamiltonian with respect to each action.
permittedResults: For a Kepler ellipse, $\varepsilon=-\mu/(2a)$ and $h=\sqrt{\mu a(1-e^2)}$.
hints: $p_r=\sqrt{2\varepsilon+2\mu/r-h^2/r^2}$ and the closed integral is twice the periapsis-to-apoapsis integral.
With $r=a(1-e\cos E)$, the integral reduces to $J_r=\sqrt{\mu a}-h$.
Invert to $H=-\mu^2/[2(J_r+h)^2]$ before taking action derivatives.
rubricCriteria: Evaluates $J_r=\mu/\sqrt{-2\varepsilon}-h=\sqrt{\mu a}[1-\sqrt{1-e^2}]$.
Derives $H=-\mu^2/[2(J_r+h)^2]$ and equal frequencies $\partial H/\partial J_r=\partial H/\partial h$.
Computes $h=5.05\times10^{10}\,\mathrm{m^2/s}$, $J_r=1.26\times10^{10}\,\mathrm{m^2/s}$, and frequency $6.31\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$.

commonErrors.description: Uses only the outward radial integral without the factor of two in the closed action.
commonErrors.consequence: The action and inferred Hamiltonian are off by a factor not absorbed by the $2\pi$ convention.

commonErrors.description: Treats $h$ as fixed before differentiating the Hamiltonian with respect to the azimuthal action.
commonErrors.consequence: The frequency degeneracy responsible for closed Kepler orbits is missed.

problems.solution: Between apsides, $p_r=\sqrt{2\varepsilon+2\mu/r-h^2/r^2}$. Evaluating the closed integral with $r=a(1-e\cos E)$ gives $J_r=\mu/\sqrt{-2\varepsilon}-h=\sqrt{\mu a}-h$. Therefore $H=-\mu^2/[2(J_r+h)^2]$, and both $\omega_r=\partial H/\partial J_r$ and $\omega_\phi=\partial H/\partial h$ equal $\mu^2/(J_r+h)^3=\sqrt{\mu/a^3}$. Numerically $\sqrt{\mu a}=6.313\times10^{10}\,\mathrm{m^2/s}$, $h=0.800\sqrt{\mu a}=5.05\times10^{10}\,\mathrm{m^2/s}$, $J_r=0.200\sqrt{\mu a}=1.26\times10^{10}\,\mathrm{m^2/s}$, and the common frequency is $6.31\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$.
problems.flawedProof: The radial action is zero for every ellipse because the particle returns to its starting radius. Hence the radial frequency vanishes while the azimuthal frequency remains finite.

problems.title: Rutherford's law follows from one impact-parameter Jacobian
problems.objective: Derive the inverse-fourth-power angular dependence of repulsive Coulomb scattering from the orbit map.
problems.statement: For repulsive central scattering in $U(r)=\kappa/r$ with kinetic energy $E>0$ at infinity, derive the relation between impact parameter $b$ and deflection angle $\Theta$, then derive $d\sigma/d\Omega$. Evaluate $b$ and $d\sigma/d\Omega$ for $\kappa=2.00\,\mathrm{J\,m}$, $E=4.00\,\mathrm J$, and $\Theta=60.0^\circ$. Check the small-angle scaling and SI dimensions.
problems.strategy: Solve or quote only after deriving the repulsive Binet hyperbola, invert its asymptotic angle to $b(\Theta)$, and apply annulus-to-solid-angle conservation.
permittedResults: For a single monotone central-scattering branch, $d\sigma/d\Omega=(b/\sin\Theta)|db/d\Theta|$.
rubricCriteria: Derives $b=(\kappa/2E)\cot(\Theta/2)$ with the repulsive sign convention made explicit.
Derives $d\sigma/d\Omega=\kappa^2[16E^2\sin^4(\Theta/2)]^{-1}$.
Computes $b=0.433\,\mathrm m$ and $d\sigma/d\Omega=0.250\,\mathrm{m^2/sr}$ and identifies the $\Theta^{-4}$ small-angle behavior.

commonErrors.description: Uses $\tan\Theta$ rather than $\tan(\Theta/2)$ in the impact map.
commonErrors.consequence: The angular singularity and numerical cross section are both wrong.

commonErrors.description: Omits the $1/\sin\Theta$ solid-angle factor.
commonErrors.consequence: The result lacks the Rutherford $\sin^{-4}(\Theta/2)$ law and has incorrect angular weighting.

problems.solution: The repulsive inverse-square Binet solution and its asymptotes give $\tan(\Theta/2)=\kappa/(2Eb)$, so $b=(\kappa/2E)\cot(\Theta/2)$. Differentiation and $d\sigma/d\Omega=(b/\sin\Theta)|db/d\Theta|$ yield $d\sigma/d\Omega=\kappa^2/[16E^2\sin^4(\Theta/2)]$. Here $\kappa/(2E)=0.250\,\mathrm m$, so $b=0.250\cot30^\circ=0.433\,\mathrm m$ and $d\sigma/d\Omega=(4/256)\csc^430^\circ=0.250\,\mathrm{m^2/sr}$. For small $\Theta$, $\sin(\Theta/2)\sim\Theta/2$, giving the $\Theta^{-4}$ scaling.
problems.flawedProof: Since the force scales as $r^{-2}$, the cross section must scale as $\Theta^{-2}$. Setting $b=\kappa/(E\tan\Theta)$ completes the derivation without a Jacobian.

problems.title: The Runge-Lenz Poisson algebra encodes Kepler geometry
problems.objective: Prove conservation and the Poisson-bracket algebra of the Laplace-Runge-Lenz vector and connect its Casimir to eccentricity.
problems.statement: For $H=\mathbf p^2/(2m)-k/r$, define $\mathbf L=\mathbf r\times\mathbf p$ and $\mathbf A=\mathbf p\times\mathbf L-mk\hat{\mathbf r}$. Using canonical Poisson brackets, prove $\{H,A_i\}=0$, derive $\{L_i,A_j\}$ and $\{A_i,A_j\}$, and show $A^2=m^2k^2+2mHL^2$. For $H<0$, identify the eccentricity and explain why $\mathbf A$ points toward periapsis. State what changes for a circular orbit.
problems.strategy: Use the rotational action of $\mathbf L$, differentiate $\mathbf A$ or bracket it with $H$, and reduce scalar products using $\mathbf p\times\mathbf L=\mathbf p^2\mathbf r-(\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf r)\mathbf p$.
hints: $d\hat{\mathbf r}/dt=[\mathbf v-(\mathbf v\cdot\hat{\mathbf r})\hat{\mathbf r}]/r$ cancels $d(\mathbf p\times\mathbf L)/dt$.
The remaining bracket is proportional to $H\epsilon_{ijk}L_k$; fix its coefficient by direct component calculation.
rubricCriteria: Proves $\dot{\mathbf A}=0$ or equivalently $\{H,A_i\}=0$ without assuming a conic orbit.
Derives $\{L_i,A_j\}=\epsilon_{ijk}A_k$ and $\{A_i,A_j\}=-2mH\epsilon_{ijk}L_k$.
Derives $A^2=m^2k^2+2mHL^2$, identifies $e=A/(mk)$, and treats the $A=0$ circular case.

commonErrors.description: Assumes $\mathbf p$ is perpendicular to $\mathbf r$ throughout an eccentric orbit.
commonErrors.consequence: Radial momentum terms are incorrectly removed from the conservation and norm calculations.

commonErrors.description: Drops the energy factor in $\{A_i,A_j\}$.
commonErrors.consequence: The bracket has wrong dimensions and fails to distinguish bound from unbound symmetry algebras.

problems.solution: Using $\dot{\mathbf p}=-(k/r^2)\hat{\mathbf r}$, $\dot{\mathbf L}=0$, and the derivative of $\hat{\mathbf r}$, one finds $d(\mathbf p\times\mathbf L)/dt=mk\,d\hat{\mathbf r}/dt$, hence $\dot{\mathbf A}=0$. Canonical component brackets give $\{L_i,A_j\}=\epsilon_{ijk}A_k$ and $\{A_i,A_j\}=-2mH\epsilon_{ijk}L_k$. Expanding $A^2$ and using $H=\mathbf p^2/(2m)-k/r$ yields $A^2=m^2k^2+2mHL^2$. Therefore the conic eccentricity is $e=A/(mk)$.
