Derive the exact Cartesian positions, kinetic energy, and potential energy, then expand through quadratic order to construct $M$ and $K$ for $q=(\theta,\delta)^T$. Prove $M>0$, solve both frequencies and ratios $\delta/\theta$, and verify mass-metric orthogonality. Finally, with zero initial velocities and $\theta(0)=0.0200\,\mathrm{rad}$, choose $\delta(0)$ to excite only the lower mode; write the resulting motion and compute its initial quadratic energy.
problems.strategy: Build the geometry using the declared relative joint angle, transform the exact energies before truncating, solve the generalized pencil, and use the desired eigenvector rather than a Euclidean projection to design the launch.
permittedResults: Distinct modes of symmetric $K$ and positive-definite $M$ satisfy $(\lambda_i-\lambda_j)v_i^TMv_j=0$.
hints: Use $\mathbf r_2=\mathbf r_1+l_2(\sin(\theta+\delta),-\cos(\theta+\delta))$ and retain the exact factor $\cos\delta$ in the velocity cross term before expanding.
The quadratic matrices are $M=\begin{pmatrix}5.5&1.5\\1.5&0.5\end{pmatrix}$ and $K=\begin{pmatrix}40&10\\10&10\end{pmatrix}$ in consistent rotational units.
For the lower mode, $\delta/\theta=(\sqrt{57}-7)/4$; choosing this ratio at rest eliminates the upper modal amplitude.
rubricCriteria: Derives the exact relative-angle geometry and energies and obtains the stated non-diagonal quadratic $M$ and $K$.
Finds $\omega^2=45\mp5\sqrt{57}$, ratios $(\sqrt{57}-7)/4$ and $-(\sqrt{57}+7)/4$, proves $M>0$, and verifies $M$-orthogonality.
Chooses $\delta(0)=2.749\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{rad}$, writes the pure lower-mode cosine motion with $\omega_-=2.693\,\mathrm{rad/s}$, and computes $E=8.59\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm J$.

commonErrors.description: Treats the declared relative angle $\delta$ as the second rod's absolute angle when constructing its position.
commonErrors.consequence: The exact velocity cross term, gravitational stiffness, generalized modes, and launch ratio all describe a different coordinate model.

commonErrors.description: Chooses the launch by an ordinary Euclidean projection while ignoring the non-diagonal kinetic metric.
commonErrors.consequence: The supposedly pure launch contains both generalized modes and develops beating.

problems.solution:
The positions are $\mathbf r_1=(l_1\sin\theta,-l_1\cos\theta)$ and $\mathbf r_2=\mathbf r_1+(l_2\sin(\theta+\delta),-l_2\cos(\theta+\delta))$. Hence
$T=\tfrac12(m_1+m_2)l_1^2\dot\theta^2+\tfrac12m_2l_2^2(\dot\theta+\dot\delta)^2+m_2l_1l_2\dot\theta(\dot\theta+\dot\delta)\cos\delta$
and $V=-(m_1+m_2)gl_1\cos\theta-m_2gl_2\cos(\theta+\delta)$. Quadratic expansion gives $M=\begin{pmatrix}5.5&1.5\\1.5&0.5\end{pmatrix}$ and $K=\begin{pmatrix}40&10\\10&10\end{pmatrix}$. Since $M_{11}=5.5>0$ and $\det M=0.5>0$, $M$ is positive definite. The determinant $\det(K-\lambda M)=300-45\lambda+\lambda^2/2$ gives $\lambda_\mp=45\mp5\sqrt{57}$ and $\omega_-=2.693\,\mathrm{rad/s}$, $\omega_+=9.097\,\mathrm{rad/s}$. Corresponding vectors $(1,d_\mp)^T$ have $d_-=(\sqrt{57}-7)/4=0.13746$ and $d_+=-(\sqrt{57}+7)/4=-3.63746$. Their mass product is $5.5+1.5(d_-+d_+)+0.5d_-d_+=0$. A pure lower launch therefore uses $\delta(0)=d_-\theta(0)=2.749\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{rad}$ and zero velocities, giving $q(t)=0.0200(1,d_-)^T\cos(2.69274t)$. Its initial energy is $q(0)^TKq(0)/2=8.588\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm J$.
problems.flawedProof: Because $\delta$ is the second coordinate, treat it as the second rod's absolute angle and write $\mathbf r_2=\mathbf r_1+l_2(\sin\delta,-\cos\delta)$. Expanding this geometry directly gives the requested relative-angle modes.

problems.title: Slow frequency drift preserves oscillator action
problems.objective: Derive the leading adiabatic invariant of a slowly varying harmonic oscillator and predict amplitude and energy scaling.
problems.statement: A harmonic oscillator has $H=p^2/(2m)+m\omega(t)^2q^2/2$ with $|\dot\omega|\ll\omega^2$. By averaging over the fast phase, show that $J=E/\omega$ is conserved to leading adiabatic order. If $m=1.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, initial $\omega_i=2.00\,\mathrm{rad/s}$, and initial amplitude $A_i=0.100\,\mathrm m$, find the final energy and amplitude after $\omega$ is slowly increased to $4.00\,\mathrm{rad/s}$. State what the invariant does not imply about phase.
problems.strategy: Differentiate energy through its explicit time dependence, replace $q^2$ by its cycle average at fixed instantaneous energy, and compare the logarithmic derivatives of $E$ and $\omega$.
permittedResults: For a harmonic cycle at energy $E$, $\langle q^2\rangle=E/(m\omega^2)$.
hints: $\dot E=\partial H/\partial t=m\omega\dot\omega q^2$ along an exact trajectory.
rubricCriteria: Derives $d(E/\omega)/dt=0$ to leading averaged order with the slow-variation condition stated.
Finds initial energy $0.0200\,\mathrm J$, final energy $0.0400\,\mathrm J$, and final amplitude $0.0707\,\mathrm m$.
Explains that action conservation does not freeze phase and accumulates only an approximate amplitude-energy relation.

commonErrors.description: Assumes energy remains constant because the oscillator is instantaneously conservative.
commonErrors.consequence: Work done by the slowly changing parameter is omitted.

commonErrors.description: Concludes amplitude scales as $1/\omega$.
commonErrors.consequence: The conserved action relation is confused with constant energy.

problems.solution: Explicit time dependence gives $\dot E=m\omega\dot\omega q^2$. Averaging one fast cycle while $\omega$ is nearly fixed yields $\langle\dot E\rangle=m\omega\dot\omega[E/(m\omega^2)]=E\dot\omega/\omega$, hence $d(E/\omega)/dt=0$ at leading adiabatic order. Initially $E_i=m\omega_i^2A_i^2/2=0.0200\,\mathrm J$. Doubling $\omega$ doubles $E$ to $0.0400\,\mathrm J$, while $A_f=A_i\sqrt{\omega_i/\omega_f}=0.0707\,\mathrm m$. The fast phase continues to advance and can acquire dynamical corrections; it is not fixed by $J$.
problems.flawedProof: Adiabatic means no work is done, so both energy and amplitude remain constant while the frequency doubles.

problems.title: The first Mathieu tongue has a controlled small-parameter boundary
problems.objective: Derive the leading first parametric-instability tongue and Floquet growth rate with an explicit asymptotic order declaration.
problems.statement: Consider Mathieu's equation $x''+[a-2q\cos(2\tau)]x=0$ with $|q|\ll1$ and $a=1+\delta$, where $\delta=O(q)$. Use a slowly varying ansatz $x=A(\tau)\cos\tau+B(\tau)\sin\tau$ with $A',B'=O(q)$ to derive the leading amplitude system, instability boundary, and Floquet exponent through errors $O(q^2)$. For $q=0.100$ and $a=1.060$, decide stability at this order and compute the growth exponent per unit $\tau$.
problems.strategy: Move detuning and modulation to the right of the unit-frequency oscillator, retain only resonant sine and cosine terms, and diagonalize the two slow-amplitude equations without extending the result beyond first order.
permittedResults: Terms at frequencies $3\tau$ average to zero in the leading slow-flow equations.
hints: The resonant balance gives $A'=(q+\delta)B/2$ and $B'=(q-\delta)A/2$ up to $O(q^2)$.
rubricCriteria: Derives the two-amplitude slow system while declaring neglected $O(q^2)$ and nonresonant terms.
Obtains first-tongue condition $|a-1|<|q|$ and growth exponent $s=\tfrac12\sqrt{q^2-(a-1)^2}+O(q^2)$.
Classifies the numerical point inside the tongue and computes $s=0.0400$ per unit $\tau$ at leading order.

commonErrors.description: Treats the modulation as ordinary additive forcing and searches for a bounded particular solution.
commonErrors.consequence: The homogeneous parametric instability mechanism is missed.

commonErrors.description: Reports the first-order tongue boundaries as exact for $q=0.100$.
commonErrors.consequence: The declared $O(q^2)$ truncation and boundary correction are concealed.

problems.solution: Writing $a=1+\delta$ gives $x''+x=-\delta x+2q\cos2\tau\,x$. With slowly varying $A,B$, the left resonant terms are $-2A'\sin\tau+2B'\cos\tau$. Retaining resonant products on the right yields $A'=(q+\delta)B/2$ and $B'=(q-\delta)A/2+O(q^2)$. Therefore $s^2=(q^2-\delta^2)/4$, so the first tongue is $|\delta|<|q|$, or $a=1\pm|q|+O(q^2)$, and $s=\tfrac12\sqrt{q^2-\delta^2}+O(q^2)$. Here $\delta=0.060$, so the point is inside and $s=\tfrac12\sqrt{0.0100-0.0036}=0.0400$ per unit $\tau$ at leading order.
problems.flawedProof: The coefficient averages to $a$, so the modulation has no effect unless $a<0$. The solution is stable because $a=1.060>0$.

problems.title: A light boundary mass creates a localized surface mode
problems.objective: Derive the existence threshold, decay factor, and frequency of an end-localized mode above a monatomic chain's bulk band.
problems.statement: A semi-infinite chain has bulk masses $m$ at sites $n=1,2,\ldots$ joined by springs $k$. The boundary mass at $n=0$ is $M$ and is joined only to site 1 by one spring $k$. Seek a mode $x_n=A\lambda^n e^{-i\omega t}$ with $|\lambda|<1$. Derive $\lambda$, the condition on $M/m$, and the localized frequency. For $m=1.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $M=0.250\,\mathrm{kg}$, and $k=100\,\mathrm{N/m}$, compute $\lambda$, $\omega$, and the localization length in lattice spacings. Verify the frequency lies above the bulk band.
problems.strategy: Use the exponential ansatz separately in the bulk and at the boundary, eliminate frequency, select the nonuniform root, and impose normalizability.
hints: Bulk motion gives $m\omega^2=k(2-\lambda-\lambda^{-1})$ and the boundary gives $M\omega^2=k(1-\lambda)$.
Besides the nonlocalized root $\lambda=1$, the root is $\lambda=\mu/(\mu-1)$ with $\mu=M/m$.
rubricCriteria: Derives $\lambda=\mu/(\mu-1)$ and localization condition $M<m/2$.
Derives $\omega^2=k/[m\mu(1-\mu)]$ and computes $\lambda=-1/3$, $\omega=23.1\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.
Computes localization length $1/|\ln|\lambda||=0.910$ lattice spacings and verifies $\omega>2\sqrt{k/m}=20.0\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.

commonErrors.description: Keeps the root $\lambda=1$ as a localized boundary mode.
commonErrors.consequence: A non-normalizable bulk-edge solution is mistaken for exponential localization.

commonErrors.description: Requires $M>m$ for localization by intuition about heavy defects.
commonErrors.consequence: The actual free-boundary condition and alternating above-band mode are reversed.

problems.solution: The bulk and boundary equations are $m\omega^2=k(2-\lambda-\lambda^{-1})$ and $M\omega^2=k(1-\lambda)$. With $\mu=M/m$, elimination gives roots $\lambda=1$ and $\lambda=\mu/(\mu-1)$. Normalizability selects the latter and requires $|\lambda|<1$, hence $0<\mu<1/2$. Substitution gives $\omega^2=k/[m\mu(1-\mu)]$. At $\mu=0.250$, $\lambda=-1/3$ and $\omega=\sqrt{533.3}=23.1\,\mathrm{rad/s}$, above the bulk ceiling $20.0\,\mathrm{rad/s}$. The amplitude localization length is $1/|\ln|\lambda||=1/\ln3=0.910$ sites.
problems.flawedProof: A surface mode must have $\lambda=1$ so all masses move together. Its frequency is therefore inside the acoustic band.

problems.title: The generalized spectral theorem builds a complete modal basis
problems.objective: Prove completeness and mass orthonormality for a symmetric small-oscillation pencil, including degenerate eigenspaces.
problems.statement: Let $M$ be real symmetric positive definite and $K$ real symmetric positive semidefinite. Prove that $Kv=\omega^2Mv$ has real nonnegative eigenvalues and a complete basis that can be chosen $M$-orthonormal. Your proof must explicitly construct a symmetric ordinary eigenproblem using $M^{1/2}$, map its eigenvectors back, and address repeated and zero eigenvalues. Derive the modal energy decomposition and state exactly what fails if $M$ is singular.
problems.strategy: Whiten the kinetic metric with the unique positive square root of $M$, apply the real symmetric spectral theorem, and transport both orthogonality and quadratic forms back to the original coordinates.
permittedResults: A real symmetric matrix has an orthonormal eigenbasis, including within each repeated eigenspace.
hints: Positive semidefiniteness of $K$ makes every Rayleigh quotient nonnegative but allows zero modes.
rubricCriteria: Constructs the symmetric whitened matrix and proves real nonnegative spectrum and completeness.
Maps an orthonormal basis back to an $M$-orthonormal basis and treats repeated and zero eigenspaces correctly.
Derives $T=\sum\dot Q_j^2/2$, $V=\sum\omega_j^2Q_j^2/2$ and explains why singular $M$ prevents this invertible whitening without prior constraint reduction.

commonErrors.description: Claims $M^{-1}K$ is symmetric in the ordinary Euclidean inner product.
commonErrors.consequence: The spectral theorem is invoked on a generally nonsymmetric matrix.

commonErrors.description: Discards zero or repeated eigenvalues as proof failures.
commonErrors.consequence: Neutral symmetries and legitimate degenerate modal subspaces are excluded from completeness.

problems.solution: Because $M>0$, its symmetric $M^{1/2}$ is invertible. Set $A=M^{-1/2}KM^{-1/2}$; then $A=A^T$ and $w^TAw=(M^{-1/2}w)^TK(M^{-1/2}w)\ge0$. The symmetric spectral theorem gives a complete Euclidean-orthonormal basis $w_j$ with real $\omega_j^2\ge0$, choosing any orthonormal basis within repeated eigenspaces. Setting $v_j=M^{-1/2}w_j$ gives $Kv_j=\omega_j^2Mv_j$ and $v_i^TMv_j=\delta_{ij}$. With $q=\sum v_jQ_j$, the quadratic energies are $T=\sum\dot Q_j^2/2$ and $V=\sum\omega_j^2Q_j^2/2$, including zero modes. If $M$ is singular, $M^{-1/2}$ does not exist; redundant or massless coordinates must be constrained or reduced first.
problems.flawedProof: $M^{-1}K$ is symmetric because both factors are symmetric. Therefore its Euclidean eigenvectors are automatically orthonormal even when $M$ is singular.

problems.title: An avoided crossing rotates modes through forty-five degrees
problems.objective: Solve a parameter-dependent two-mode avoided crossing and quantify its minimum gap and mode mixing.
problems.statement: For unit modal mass, let $K(s)=\omega_0^2I+\begin{pmatrix}\alpha s&g\\g&-\alpha s\end{pmatrix}$ with $g>0$. Derive exact squared frequencies and a mixing angle $\theta(s)$ relating instantaneous modes to the coordinate axes. Find the minimum squared-frequency gap and show how mode identities exchange as $s$ passes through zero. Evaluate frequencies at $s=0$ and $s=1$ for $\omega_0=10.0\,\mathrm{rad/s}$, $\alpha=3.00\,\mathrm{s^{-2}}$, and $g=4.00\,\mathrm{s^{-2}}$.
problems.strategy: Diagonalize the traceless two-by-two perturbation exactly, parameterize its eigenvectors by a rotation, and inspect asymptotic eigenvector limits on both sides of the crossing.
hints: A consistent mixing convention satisfies $\tan2\theta=g/(\alpha s)$ with quadrant chosen continuously.
At $s=0$, the eigenvectors are equal and opposite coordinate combinations.
rubricCriteria: Derives the exact eigenvalues and a quadrant-consistent mixing-angle relation.
Finds minimum squared-frequency gap $2g$ at $s=0$ and explains the exchange of coordinate character.
Computes frequencies $9.798,10.198\,\mathrm{rad/s}$ at $s=0$ and $9.747,10.247\,\mathrm{rad/s}$ at $s=1$.

commonErrors.description: Sets $g=0$ when locating the crossing and reports exact degeneracy at $s=0$.
commonErrors.consequence: The coupling responsible for the avoided gap is removed.

commonErrors.description: Uses $\tan\theta=g/(\alpha s)$ instead of the double-angle diagonalization relation.
commonErrors.consequence: The predicted mode rotation is incorrect near the crossing.

problems.solution: The traceless part has eigenvalues $\pm\sqrt{\alpha^2s^2+g^2}$, so $\omega_\pm^2=\omega_0^2\pm\sqrt{\alpha^2s^2+g^2}$. A continuous rotation can be chosen with $\tan2\theta=g/(\alpha s)$ using $\operatorname{atan2}(g,\alpha s)$; at $s=0$, $\theta=\pi/4$. The squared-frequency gap is $2\sqrt{\alpha^2s^2+g^2}$, minimized at $2g$. As $s$ changes sign, the eigenvectors exchange their dominant coordinate component. Numerically, at $s=0$ the frequencies are $\sqrt{96}=9.798$ and $\sqrt{104}=10.198\,\mathrm{rad/s}$; at $s=1$ they are $\sqrt{95}=9.747$ and $\sqrt{105}=10.247\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.
problems.flawedProof: The diagonal entries cross at $s=0$, so the exact frequencies are equal there. Off-diagonal coupling changes only eigenvectors, not eigenvalues.

problems.title: Alternating springs support a midgap edge mode
problems.objective: Construct and normalize an exponentially localized edge mode in a dimerized mechanical chain.
problems.statement: A semi-infinite chain has equal masses $m$ with cell coordinates $A_n,B_n$. Intracell springs have stiffness $k_1$ and intercell springs have stiffness $k_2$; the left $A_1$ site is additionally tethered by $k_2$ so every bulk and boundary diagonal stiffness is $k_1+k_2$. Seek a mode at $\omega_e^2=(k_1+k_2)/m$ with $B_n=0$. Derive its $A_n$ profile, localization condition, mass normalization, and localization length. Evaluate for $m=1.00\,\mathrm{kg}$, $k_1=1.00\,\mathrm{N/m}$, and $k_2=4.00\,\mathrm{N/m}$.
problems.strategy: Subtract the common diagonal term at the midgap frequency, solve the remaining off-diagonal recurrence, impose square summability, and normalize the resulting geometric series.
hints: $A_{n+1}=-(k_1/k_2)A_n$, so localization at the left requires $k_1<k_2$.
For unit total modal mass, $|A_1|=\sqrt{(1-r^2)/m}$ with $r=k_1/k_2$.
rubricCriteria: Derives $A_n=A_1(-k_1/k_2)^{n-1}$ and the condition $k_1<k_2$.
Normalizes the mode and derives localization length $\xi=1/\ln(k_2/k_1)$ cells.
Computes $\omega_e=\sqrt5=2.236\,\mathrm{rad/s}$, $A_{n+1}/A_n=-0.250$, $|A_1|=0.968\,\mathrm{kg^{-1/2}}$, and $\xi=0.721$ cells.

commonErrors.description: Uses ratio $-k_2/k_1$ for a left-localized mode when $k_2>k_1$.
commonErrors.consequence: The amplitude grows into the bulk and is not normalizable.

commonErrors.description: Omits the declared boundary tether while retaining the uniform diagonal midgap frequency.
commonErrors.consequence: The boundary equation no longer supports the proposed exact mode.

problems.solution: At $m\omega_e^2=k_1+k_2$, the diagonal term cancels. Setting $B_n=0$, the $B_n$ equation gives $k_1A_n+k_2A_{n+1}=0$, so $A_n=A_1(-k_1/k_2)^{n-1}$. Square summability requires $k_1/k_2<1$. Unit modal mass gives $m|A_1|^2/[1-(k_1/k_2)^2]=1$, and the amplitude decay length is $\xi=1/\ln(k_2/k_1)$. Here $\omega_e=\sqrt5=2.236\,\mathrm{rad/s}$, the ratio is $-0.250$, $|A_1|=\sqrt{15/16}=0.968\,\mathrm{kg^{-1/2}}$, and $\xi=1/\ln4=0.721$ cells.
problems.flawedProof: Localization requires the stronger spring to be inside each cell, so $A_n=(-k_2/k_1)^{n-1}$ and the growing amplitude is acceptable in an infinite chain.

problems.title: The modal resolvent exposes every driven resonance
problems.objective: Derive the Green-matrix expansion of an undamped finite system and verify it against direct inversion.
problems.statement: For symmetric positive-definite $M,K$ with $M$-orthonormal modes $v_j$, derive the harmonic response to $f e^{-i\Omega t}$ as a modal resolvent. State the pole and residue structure and the solvability condition exactly at an eigenfrequency. Then use $M=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$, $K=\begin{pmatrix}5&-1\\-1&5\end{pmatrix}$, $f=(1,0)^T\,\mathrm N$, and $\Omega=2.00\,\mathrm{rad/s}$ to compute the displacement amplitude by both modal expansion and direct inversion.
problems.strategy: Use modal completeness $VV^T=M^{-1}$ to invert the dynamic stiffness, identify rank-one residues, and confirm the numerical response with the original matrices.
permittedResults: The steady amplitude satisfies $(K-\Omega^2M)Q=f$ away from resonance.
hints: The example has squared frequencies $4/3$ and $6$.
rubricCriteria: Derives the rank-one modal Green expansion using the correct $M$ normalization.
Identifies simple poles and states that resonant forcing must be orthogonal to the resonant mode for a bounded particular solution in the ideal undamped model.
Computes $Q=(0.1875,-0.3125)^T\,\mathrm m$ by both methods.

commonErrors.description: Uses $v_jv_j^TM$ in the resolvent numerator after already mass-normalizing modes.
commonErrors.consequence: The proposed inverse fails when multiplied by the dynamic stiffness.

commonErrors.description: Assigns a finite steady amplitude at a resonant pole for arbitrary forcing in an undamped system.
commonErrors.consequence: Secular growth and the Fredholm compatibility condition are ignored.

problems.solution: If $V^TMV=I$ and $KV=MV\Omega_d^2$, completeness gives $VV^T=M^{-1}$. Hence $(K-\Omega^2M)^{-1}=\sum_jv_jv_j^T/(\omega_j^2-\Omega^2)$. Each simple pole has rank-one residue proportional to $v_jv_j^T$; at $\Omega=\omega_j$, a bounded harmonic particular solution exists only if $v_j^Tf=0$. In the example, direct inversion of $[[-3,-5],[-5,-3]]$ gives $Q=(0.1875,-0.3125)^T\,\mathrm m$. Using the normalized symmetric and antisymmetric modes with denominators $4/3-4$ and $6-4$ gives the same vector.
problems.flawedProof: The resolvent is $\sum_j v_jv_j^TM/(\omega_j^2-\Omega^2)$ because completeness contains $M$. Multiplying the force by this expression gives the response.

problems.title: A complete target spectrum reconstructs a spring network
problems.objective: Solve an inverse normal-mode problem and decide whether the reconstructed stiffness is realizable by positive springs.
problems.statement: Three unit masses must have orthonormal modes $v_1=(1,1,1)^T/\sqrt3$, $v_2=(1,0,-1)^T/\sqrt2$, and $v_3=(1,-2,1)^T/\sqrt6$ at frequencies $1,2,3\,\mathrm{rad/s}$, respectively. Reconstruct the unique symmetric stiffness matrix. Interpret each negative off-diagonal entry as a pair spring and each row sum as a ground spring. Verify all spring constants are nonnegative, recover the spectrum directly, and explain what information would be insufficient if only the three frequencies were prescribed.
problems.strategy: Use the complete spectral decomposition $K=V\operatorname{diag}(\omega_j^2)V^T$, then translate matrix signs and row sums into network elements.
permittedResults: For unit mass and a complete orthonormal mode matrix, $K=\sum_j\omega_j^2v_jv_j^T$.
hints: The off-diagonal entries are $-8/3,-8/3,-1/6$ for pairs $(1,2),(2,3),(1,3)$.
Each row sum equals the corresponding ground stiffness.
rubricCriteria: Constructs the unique matrix $K=\sum_j\omega_j^2v_jv_j^T$ from the full signed modal data.
Extracts pair springs $8/3,8/3,1/6\,\mathrm{N/m}$ and ground springs $1,1,1\,\mathrm{N/m}$, all nonnegative.
Verifies the target eigenpairs and explains that eigenvalues alone leave an arbitrary orthogonal eigenbasis and therefore many possible networks.

commonErrors.description: Builds $K$ with frequencies rather than squared frequencies.
commonErrors.consequence: The target eigenvalues and physical units are wrong.

commonErrors.description: Reads diagonal entries directly as ground spring constants.
commonErrors.consequence: Contributions from pair springs are double-counted and the reconstructed network is incorrect.

problems.solution: $K=1v_1v_1^T+4v_2v_2^T+9v_3v_3^T=\begin{pmatrix}23/6&-8/3&-1/6\\-8/3&19/3&-8/3\\-1/6&-8/3&23/6\end{pmatrix}\,\mathrm{N/m}$. Thus pair springs are $k_{12}=k_{23}=8/3$ and $k_{13}=1/6\,\mathrm{N/m}$. Row sums are all $1$, so each mass also has a $1\,\mathrm{N/m}$ ground spring. These nonnegative elements reconstruct the matrix. Multiplication by each $v_j$ returns eigenvalues $1,4,9\,\mathrm{s^{-2}}$. Frequencies alone would not specify the orthogonal eigenvectors, so they would not determine a unique $K$ or topology.
problems.flawedProof: The stiffness matrix is simply $\operatorname{diag}(1,2,3)$ because those are the requested frequencies. Mode shapes do not affect network design.

problems.title: Coupled nonlinear normal modes split beyond linear degeneracy
problems.objective: Identify invariant nonlinear mode lines in a symmetric two-coordinate oscillator and compare their leading amplitude-dependent frequencies.
problems.statement: Unit masses move in $V=\tfrac12\omega_0^2(x^2+y^2)+\tfrac14\alpha(x^4+y^4)+\tfrac12\beta x^2y^2$, with $\omega_0>0$. Prove that $y=0$ and $y=\pm x$ are invariant nonlinear normal-mode subspaces for compatible initial velocities. Derive the scalar equation on each and use a Lindstedt expansion through $O(A^2)$ to find the frequency at coordinate amplitude $A$. Evaluate the axial and diagonal frequencies for $\omega_0=4.00\,\mathrm{rad/s}$, $\alpha=40.0\,\mathrm{s^{-2}m^{-2}}$, $\beta=80.0\,\mathrm{s^{-2}m^{-2}}$, and $A=0.100\,\mathrm m$. State the smallness checks.
problems.strategy: Verify invariance directly in both equations, reduce each subspace to a Duffing equation, and remove the resonant third-order term by adjusting the oscillation frequency.
hints: On the axis, the cubic coefficient is $\gamma=\alpha$.
On either diagonal with $x=y=s$, the coefficient is $\gamma=\alpha+\beta$.
Check $\gamma A^2/\omega_0^2\ll1$ separately for the two branches.
rubricCriteria: Proves the three invariant subspaces and derives their scalar Duffing equations.
Obtains axial shift $3\alpha A^2/(8\omega_0)$ and diagonal shift $3(\alpha+\beta)A^2/(8\omega_0)$.
Computes $4.0375$ and $4.1125\,\mathrm{rad/s}$ and reports small parameters $0.025$ and $0.075$.

commonErrors.description: Uses the linear superposition principle to combine arbitrary nonlinear mode motions.
commonErrors.consequence: Invariant nonlinear subspaces are confused with a global linear basis.

commonErrors.description: Uses coefficient $2\beta$ on the diagonal without differentiating the potential.
commonErrors.consequence: The amplitude-dependent diagonal frequency is over-shifted.

problems.solution: The equations are $x''+\omega_0^2x+\alpha x^3+\beta xy^2=0$ and $y''+\omega_0^2y+\alpha y^3+\beta x^2y=0$. They preserve $y=0$ and $y=\pm x$ when velocities satisfy the same relation. On the axis, $x''+\omega_0^2x+\alpha x^3=0$; on a diagonal, $s''+\omega_0^2s+(\alpha+\beta)s^3=0$. Lindstedt expansion gives $\omega_{\mathrm{axis}}=\omega_0+3\alpha A^2/(8\omega_0)=4.0375\,\mathrm{rad/s}$ and $\omega_{\mathrm{diag}}=\omega_0+3(\alpha+\beta)A^2/(8\omega_0)=4.1125\,\mathrm{rad/s}$. The expansion parameters are $\alpha A^2/\omega_0^2=0.025$ and $(\alpha+\beta)A^2/\omega_0^2=0.075$.
problems.flawedProof: Linear degeneracy means every line through the origin remains an exact nonlinear mode with the same frequency at all amplitudes.

problems.title: Balanced gain and loss coalesce at an exceptional point
problems.objective: Locate the eigenvalue and eigenvector coalescence of a two-oscillator quadratic pencil with balanced gain and loss.
problems.statement: Consider $\ddot x+2\gamma\dot x+\omega_0^2x+\kappa y=0$ and $\ddot y-2\gamma\dot y+\omega_0^2y+\kappa x=0$, where $\gamma>0$ and $\kappa$ has units $\mathrm{s^{-2}}$. For harmonic motion $e^{-i\omega t}$, derive the equation for $z=\omega^2$, find the exceptional-point condition where its two roots coalesce, and find the coalesced frequency. Evaluate the positive exceptional coupling and frequency for $\omega_0=5.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and $\gamma=1.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. Explain why this non-Hermitian system is not covered by the conservative spectral theorem.
problems.strategy: Form the complex dynamic matrix, reduce its determinant to a real quadratic in squared frequency, set the discriminant to zero, and inspect eigenvector rank at the repeated root.
permittedResults: An exceptional point requires both eigenvalue coincidence and loss of a complete eigenvector basis.
rubricCriteria: Derives the quadratic in $z$ and the discriminant condition with consistent units.
Finds $\kappa_{\mathrm{EP}}=2\gamma\sqrt{\omega_0^2-\gamma^2}$ and $\omega_{\mathrm{EP}}=\sqrt{\omega_0^2-2\gamma^2}$ in the real-frequency regime.
Computes $\kappa_{\mathrm{EP}}=9.80\,\mathrm{s^{-2}}$ and $\omega_{\mathrm{EP}}=4.80\,\mathrm{rad/s}$ and explains eigenvector coalescence and non-Hermiticity.

commonErrors.description: Sets only the two diagonal frequencies equal and calls that an exceptional point.
commonErrors.consequence: The coupling, damping, and eigenvector defect are ignored.

commonErrors.description: Applies the positive-definite conservative modal theorem despite one coordinate having gain.
commonErrors.consequence: A non-self-adjoint quadratic pencil is falsely assigned an orthogonal complete basis.

problems.solution: The harmonic dynamic matrix has diagonal entries $\omega_0^2-z\mp2i\gamma\sqrt z$ and off-diagonal $\kappa$. Its determinant gives $z^2+(4\gamma^2-2\omega_0^2)z+\omega_0^4-\kappa^2=0$. Vanishing discriminant yields $\kappa_{\mathrm{EP}}^2=4\gamma^2(\omega_0^2-\gamma^2)$, and the repeated root is $z_{\mathrm{EP}}=\omega_0^2-2\gamma^2$. At that root the two dynamic-matrix rows become dependent with a one-dimensional nullspace, so eigenvectors coalesce. Numerically $\kappa_{\mathrm{EP}}=2\sqrt{24}=9.80\,\mathrm{s^{-2}}$ and $\omega_{\mathrm{EP}}=\sqrt{23}=4.80\,\mathrm{rad/s}$. Balanced gain and loss make the pencil non-Hermitian, outside the conservative $M,K$ spectral theorem.
problems.flawedProof: Both uncoupled diagonal frequencies equal $\omega_0$, so they are already degenerate. Declare $\kappa=0$ an exceptional point without checking the discriminant or whether two eigenvectors coalesce.

problems.title: A switched oscillator is unstable although each stage is stable
problems.objective: Construct a monodromy matrix for piecewise-stable oscillation and decide Floquet stability from its trace and multipliers.
problems.statement: An oscillator alternates periodically between $x''+\omega_1^2x=0$ for duration $t_1$ and $x''+\omega_2^2x=0$ for duration $t_2$. Derive the phase-space propagator for one constant-frequency segment and the one-period monodromy matrix. Prove its determinant is one and state the trace stability criterion. Evaluate for $\omega_1=1.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, $t_1=\pi/2\,\mathrm s$, $\omega_2=2.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, and $t_2=\pi/4\,\mathrm s$. Find the Floquet multipliers and exponential growth rate per unit physical time.
problems.strategy: Propagate the state vector $(x,\dot x)$ through each interval in chronological order, multiply the two symplectic matrices, and classify reciprocal multipliers from the trace.
permittedResults: For a real $2\times2$ matrix with determinant one, bounded Floquet multipliers lie on the unit circle when $|\operatorname{tr}M|<2$.
hints: Both stages advance by a quarter cycle, so $P_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $P_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&1/2\\-2&0\end{pmatrix}$.
rubricCriteria: Derives the segment propagator, chronological monodromy product, and unit determinant.
Finds $M=\operatorname{diag}(-1/2,-2)$, trace $-2.5$, and multipliers $-1/2,-2$, hence instability.
Computes period $3\pi/4\,\mathrm s$ and growth rate $\ln2/(3\pi/4)=0.294\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, explaining why stable stages can compose unstably.

commonErrors.description: Adds the two segment propagators instead of composing them.
commonErrors.consequence: The result is not a time-evolution map and need not have determinant one.

commonErrors.description: Declares stability because each constant-frequency interval is individually stable.
commonErrors.consequence: Parametric energy pumping through the switching sequence is overlooked.

problems.solution: For state $(x,\dot x)^T$, a constant segment has $P(\omega,t)$ as stated and $\det P=1$, so the monodromy $M=P_2P_1$ also has determinant one. With both phase advances $\pi/2$, $P_1=[[0,1],[-1,0]]$ and $P_2=[[0,1/2],[-2,0]]$, hence $M=\operatorname{diag}(-1/2,-2)$. Its trace is $-2.5$, outside the stable interval, and its reciprocal multipliers are $-1/2$ and $-2$. One cycle lasts $T=\pi/2+\pi/4=3\pi/4\,\mathrm s$, so the growing multiplier gives rate $\ln2/T=0.294\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. Stable segment flows can pump energy when their phase-space squeezes are composed.
problems.flawedProof: Combine the two stages by addition: $M=P(\omega_1,t_1)+P(\omega_2,t_2)$. Its eigenvalues are the Floquet multipliers because addition superposes the elapsed time intervals.
